speechtext:
I wish to refer to a return
[Mr. Stevens.)
brought down on Friday evening, for the purpose of asking a question of the ministry. The return embodies the correspondence relating to the recent signing of the Halibut Fisheries Treaty. By the return it is disclosed that the government has attempted to make a treaty binding only on the inhabitants and nationals of Canada on our part and on the inhabitants and nationals of the United States on the other, and it appears that in respect of the execution-the negotiations having been, properly, conducted by the Dominion-the courtesy of signature by the British Ambassador was denied by the Prime Minister and denied in the name of Canada. The result of the terms of the treaty and of its execution in this new fangled manner appears to have been a rider on the part of the United States Senate in its resolution of ratification, which rider provides that the treaty shall be applicable on our part as respects not only our nationals and our inhabitants but as respects also those of Great Britain. What I wish to put to the government is this: as the correspondence, according to the file brought down, closed on the fifth of March, and as the United States ratification is conditional on its application to Great Britain, whose sanction, of course, does not appear, owing to the absence of any signature representing the British government, what is the present position of the treaty? Will there be a treaty upon ratification by this House, and what is the intention of the government as respects the United States Senate's proviso on ratification?

speakeroldname: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I do not think that what my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) has called the rider will create any difficulty as to the ratification of the treaty. The United States senate ratified the treaty on the understanding that the nationals of "other parts of Great Britain"-the . phraseology is rather queer-would also be prevented from fishing for halibut in those waters. This is very easy to do. As far as the territorial waters are concerned both countries, the United States and Canada, will by legislation prevent any halibut fishing. As far as the extra-territorial waters are concerned no vessel from any country can carry on halibut fishing without using either United States or Canadian ports. It will be easy in the legislation which will have to be enacted by the United States Congress and by the parliament of Canada to close Canadian and American ports to any vessel carrying on halibut fishing. Consequently, I do not see any difficulty in the ratification of the treaty.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. James Larkin was rejected at Highwater, P.Q., on the 13th instant because he refused to answer questions put by the examining officer. He was rejected because of refusal to answer the

ordinary questions that are asked those seeking admission to Canada. He appealed, and I was somewhat doubtful whether the proper grounds had been taken. I consulted with the Justice department, who are of the opinion that Mr. Larkin was properly rejected under subsection 2 of section 33 of the Immigration Act, which reads as follows:
Every passenger or other person seeking to enter or land in Canada shall answer truly all questions put to him by any officer when examined under the authority of this act, and any person not truly answering such questions shall be guilty of an offence and liable on conviction to a fine of not more than one hundred dollars or to a tenn of imprisonment, and if found not to be a Canadian citizen or not to have Canadian domicile, such offence shall in itself be sufficient cause for deportation whenever so ordered by a board of inquiry or officer in charge, subject, however, to such right of appeal as he may have to the minister.
The Justice department found we were quite correct in our contention. In addition, Mr. Larkin had just been released from serving a prison sentence, and on that ground I confirmed his rejection.

Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) moved that the' House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved that it is expedient to revise the law relating to banking, to continue until the first day of July, 1933, the charters of the several banks to which the provisions of the Bank Act apply, to authorize the payment out of Consolidated Revenue Fund of remuneration to auditors for special examinations of the affairs or business of banks which the Minister of Finance may require to be made, and to provide for the charge of fees in connection with the registration of securities taken under the authority of the provisions of the act.
Motion agreed to and House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution before you is a formality, necessary under our parliamentary practice, as the basis of a bill which is to be introduced immediately on the adoption of the resolution. I think, perhaps, the House will be conveni-enced if I proceed at once, on the motion before us, to state the nature of the bill which I shall have the pleasure of introducing shortly. In that measure the government will bring the best possible judgment they can to bear upon a question of the highest importance, and one of wide-spread interest. I cannot venture the hope that the conclusions we have reached will be received with unanimity. I am well aware that the question is one concerning which there there will be differences of opinion, but I am going to ask, and I think it reasonable to do so, that hon. gentlemen reserve their judgment in the mat-

ter, until they have had an opportunity of examining the bill, and, what perhaps is of more importance, an opportunity of participating in or observing the inquiry which will take place before the committee on Banking and Commerce. So soon as the early stages of this bill are disposed of, it is my intention to ask the House to refer the bill to the committee on Banking and Commerce, where there will be abundant opportunity for raising every question in relation to it, and the fullest possible opportunity for inquiry and discussion.
The Bank Act is the fruit of the study of a long line of ministers of finance, of governments and parliaments, and I feel that in the main it has served a good purpose; it has proved itself adapted to the needs of Canada; . and I venture the opinion-which, possibly, will not be shared by everybody-that any radical change in the act at present would have a disturbing effect upon the business of the country; it is a class of question upon which we shall do well, I think to go slowly.
At every revision of the Bank" Act a question of paramount importance has been raised concerning government inspection. Every minister of finance who has preceded me has, after consideration, reached the conclusion that it was not wise to adopt a system of government inspection. I have myself-in my own experience where I have had to do with a former revision-taken that view, and I adhere to that view at present. With our wide-spread system of branch banks any adequate system of inspection would call for a small army of officials; it would involve large expenditure, and my own impression is, that in the end you would have no better guarantee of the soundness of a bank, after government inspection, than you have under the present system. If the auditors who passed on the affairs of the Merchants bank had had a label on their caps denoting that they were government officials I have no reason to suppose that they would have been more capable, more intelligent, or more energetic.
I have great respect for government authority in some cases, but it may be overdone. I do not believe government inspection would give you any greater real protection than you now have, but it would, I think, give a false security, it would create the impression in the minds of the people that the government were guaranteeing the transactions of a bank, and whenever trouble might occur-and it is worth while remembering that where government inspection prevails bank failures are not rare-wherever trouble might occur and a bank failed, then, if you had a system of

Bank Act Revision
government inspection, there would unquestionably be a desire to hold the government responsible. Embarrassment and trouble, perhaps material loss to the government, would follow. In declining at present to concur in the idea of government inspection I want to protect the public-that is the people at large, and parliament-against the responsibility which I think they should not be willing to bear. So, after much reflection and with the knowledge that that is one of the big questions of the day, I am not of the opinion that we should advise parliament to adopt a system of government inspection.
I have said that I believe the general framework of the Bank Act is a good one. Nevertheless, with every revision we learn something. We have learned something undoubtedly during the past ten years, and we will endeavour, in the suggestions we offer, to show that the lessons of these years have not been lost. We will endeavour to improve the Bank Act while not making any radical departure from its general outline.
While we are not going to adopt a system of government inspection, we will endeavour to improve the present system of audit, and I think that is an important point. The present system of audit, shareholders' audit, is that a list of proposed auditors is prepared by the Canadian Bankers' Association and sent to the Minister of Finance. He has the right to strike off from that list any name of which he may not approve. I am proposing to adhere largely to that system but to make it, I think, more rigid, so that the public will have a better audit, a better guarantee of audit, than they have at present. Under the law of to-day the Bankers' Association forwards this list of persons who desire to be auditors, but there is no particular qualification required of them. I propose that the Bankers' Association shall still prepare a list, but that that list shall be confined strictly to chartered accountants; that those who are to act as auditors for the shareholders must be chartered accountants, and must have practised their profession as chartered accountants for a period of six years in a city or town in Canada where there is a head office of a bank. I think when we put that condition in we go a long way towards obtaining capable auditors. Many of the firms of chartered accountants comprise quite a number of members. I propose that in no case shall more than three members of any one firm be allowed to have a place on that list. We think that in this way we shall get capable auditors, members of the Chartered Accountants' Association of Canada. I believe there are chartered accountants' organizations in the various provinces, and they are federated into a Dominion association. We propose that the Dominion association shall supply a list of the members who are eligible under the condition I have laid down. I think it will necessarily follow that if you take chartered accountants who have been practising their profession for some years in one of our cities where there is the head office of a bank you have a reasonable assurance that you will obtain capable men of good standing. I think in that respect we shall give to the House and to the public a better guarantee of audit than we now have. We propose that every bank must have two auditors; under the Bank Act to-day you may have one or more. We propose that there shall be two auditors chosen by the shareholders, and that they shall not both be members of the one firm, they must belong to different firms; and they shall not be auditors for the one bank for more than three years in succession. We think these several suggestions will give to the public a guarantee that the auditors will be capable, that they will be independent; and the auditors will be changed with sufficient frequency to guard against anything going wrong.
Another question that is of very much importance, upon which I am going to make, shall I say?-a disappointing remark, is in relation to bank mergers. Bank mergers are not popular. The merger of any two banks, particularly the merger of two of the larger banks, undoubtedly makes towards a restriction of banking operation. It tends towards the creation, if there be such a thing, of a banking monopoly. I know that usually bank mergers are not popular. I know that more than one suggestion has been offered that no bank should be allowed to amalgamate with another unless they obtain authority by a special act of parliament. Some members may be disposed to approve of that suggestion; my own judgment is that it is too drastic a change. There are times when mergers may be useful, and not only that but I know of a case where a bank was beginning to get into trouble, but the matter being taken up in time it was amalgamated with another bank, the situation was saved and ail went well. So I think there will be occasions when, if you do not use the power which exists under the present law to authorize a merger through the Treasury Board, the Minister of Finance, and the Governor in Council, you may have a financial disaster which could have been avoided had you dealt with the situation in time. I am willing to have the matter fully threshed out before the Banking
Bank Act Revision

and Commerce committee, but my impres-' sion is that you must trust the government of the day, the Minister of Finance of the day and the Treasury Board, to exercise due precaution and to see that mergers are not approved of, unless they are clearly and undoubtedly in the public interests. I am persuaded that to deny the government, and the Minister of Finance and the Treasury Board that power and to say that there can be no merger until you have a special act of parliament, is an arrangement that would not work well and might at times prevent a merger which is really desirable and necessary in the interests of the public. On this point there may be disappointment in some quarters. When we talk about protecting the public in banking matters, we had better stop and think, who are the public we want to protect? There are various interests in the public, when we use that word.
In the first.place, you have the note-holders. If the government and the parliament of Canada give to the bank the right to issue notes for circulation, then surely the government and the parliament of Canada must take measures to sec that the notes are protected. That is done; the notes to-day are secured in two ways. In the first place, they are a first charge upon all the assets of the bank, and that is usually almost in itself a sufficient protection. Then, besides, there is an insurance fund created by all the banks, to which they all contribute in order to create an additional guarantee that the notes will be protected. Thus the notes are protected, I think I may safely say, beyond any question. [DOT] Then you have the depositors. They are not as well protected as the note holders. The protection in the case of the depositors is the protection given tp any creditors who have a claim against the bank. But then you have besides the double liability of the shareholders, which stands between the depositors and loss. In most cases it will be found that the existing provisions with regard to depositors work fairly well. If something can be found in the course of discussion which is better than these provisions I am willing to receive it with an open mind. The depositors do not often suffer. There have been eight bank failures in the last 20 years. In the case of five of those failures the depositors never lost a penny. In three of those failures the banks which were smaller institutions, are still in liquidation, but the depositors stand to lose. I think it is desirable we should protect the depositors, and if anybody can suggest, in the course of the inquiry, any better method of protecting the ^Mr. Fielding.]
depositor, I am quite willing to receive it and give it duo consideration, though I do not think there is as much danger of the depositors losing now as in former days. However, that is a fair matter for consideration.
^ ou come then to the shareholders, who are the bank. The shareholder is not exactly in the same position as the depositor. He is the trustee of the depositor, He is after all only a member of a trading corporation, and I think we have as much reason to ask the shareholder in the bank to look after his own interests as we have to ask the shareholder in any other corporation to do so. We are giving the shareholders-that is the banks-large privileges in the way of circulation, but I do not think that creates a special obligation whereby we should look after them, except in the general way that all corporations are supposed to have the protection of our laws. I do not think we can undertake to make the shareholder's position as good as we do the position of the note-holders or the depositors. I am afraid the shareholder must be asked, as in any other corporation, to look after his own interests as much as he can, and not to expect the government to give him exceptional and special protection.
There is another clause in the Bank Act which has given rise to much discussion, commonly known as section 88. That section gives a prior lien to the bank in certain cases. There has been much discussion of that clause in time past. There has been much criticism even in Canada, and outside of Canada it has frequently been the subject of criticism. It is claimed that the merchant abroad-and it might be true of those at home-who sells goods to a merchant in Canada, and is not able to look after his own interests, finds, when trouble occurs, that the bank has prior claim to everything. When the unpaid vendor comes to assert his claim, he finds the bank, by its prior right, has possession of the goods. When I was in England recently I was waited upon, by a deputation of the Bradford Chamber of Commerce, who made strong representations in that respect. They claimed that many English exporters had suffered severely in recent years.
I think some measure of their loss was probably due to their rather reckless method of selling. However, there is some room for criticism in the fact that the bank has priority. There are men who would advocate the total abolition of section 88. ,1 do not think such a course would be wise. That provision has performed a large and important part in the development of Canadian business, and I believe the repeal of that clause would work

Bank Act Revision
injuriously. What I am proposing now is not to repeal the clause, but that he who desires to operate under section 88 shall give notice in a public way, so that all who are concerned shall know what he is doing. I propose that any merchant or manufacturer in Canada who desires to borrow from the bank under the provisions of section 88-that is the provision which will give the bank a prior claim-must give notice in the registry office of his intention to do so. The registrar will be the Assistant Receiver General in each province. The bank will see that he registers, otherwise they will not give him the money. If the merchant at home or abroad is concerned about section 88, all he has to do is to write or telegraph to the Assistant Receiver General in the province and ascertain whether any registration has been made. If the man who is proposing to do business has been registered under section 88, all who do business with him will know that they must recognize the priority of the bank. If he gives no such notice, the bank will have no priority. I hope we shall go a long way in removing the criticisms that have been made of this section 88.
There have been questions regarding the allotment of stock, by a bank. It has been alleged in some cases that it has been contemplated that stock dividends should be declared. I do not think it has actually been done. The question has been raised whether dividends of that kind could be declared. We propose to make it clear that, whatever stock of that kind is issued and allotted, the shareholder who purchases the stock must pay in cash, and that no stock dividends shall be allowed.
There are quite a number of small amendments with which I shall not deal. Amendments will be printed in the bill in italics when it is presented to the House. I do not think I had better detain the House by referring to more than the important see [DOT] tions. There are some clauses which have become obsolete, and which are omitted. For example, there is the clause respecting the bank of British North America, which was an institution operating under exceptional conditions. That institution has been amalgamated with another bank, and so the conditions regarding it no longer exist. There were also provisions regarding fifty-dollar shares, which are no longer necessary, as the banks now generally conform to the custom of issuing hundred-dollar shares. In the returns that are made showing the banks' property we are asking a change, we are asking that the bank, in dealing with the value of their property shall include not only the
property which stands in their name, but the property which stands in the name of any corporation which they control. The banks have formed subsidiary companies which are practically branches of the bank and controlled by the bank in every way. We propose that, as respects the holding of property and as respects assets and liabilities, the returns shall show the operation of these companies the same as the operation of what I may call the bank proper. That will apply to any corporation that is controlled by the bank.
Most of the banks now have a pension fund for their employees-I am not sure whether they all have. It was found in the case of a recent bank failure that moneys designed to protect the pension fund were invested in bank stock, and when the bank stock took a tumble, the pension fund took a tumble, too. We propose that hereafter banks having pension funds shall not be permitted to invest money for the pension fund in stock of their own bank or any other bank whatsoever.
As regards bank directors, it is sometimes said that "directors do not direct." There are cases in which men who have long and honourable association with a bank desire to have their names retained on the board of directors, even when they have reached a condition where it is well known that they are not able to give close attention. I think there is an honourable purpose in that, and I would not say that it should not be done. We are proposing to introduce a clause to the effect that a record shall be kept of every bank board meeting, showing what directors have attended the meeting, and that before the next annual meeting is called upon to elect directors, that record, showing how many meetings were held and how many meetings each director attended, should be placed in the hands of the shareholders, who can then judge whether they wish to continue those directors in the service.
Some troubles have arisen owing to officials of a bank kindly lending themselves the bank's funds. We propose an amendment by which we declare that no general manager, assistant general manager, bank manager or any official, clerk or servant, can have a loan exceeding $1,000 without the consent of the directors, and he cannot have more than $10,000 even with the consent of the directors. If a bank manager or any one associated with him wants to do a little speculation, he will have to go to another bank and not get the funds out of his own bank.
There is one other provision of some importance. The bank law says, and has said for many years, that the word "bank" shall
Bank Act Revision

not be used by any person or corporation other than a chartered bank. This is a wise precaution. But though the word "bank" cannot be legally used, there are men engaged in what is practically banking business, who do not come within the operation of the law, and more than once disastrous failures have occurred. One occurred in Winnipeg within the last few weeks, where a corporation having no bank charter was actually doing a banking business with disastrous results. We are proposing that whoever desires to receive money on deposit in Canada, shall obtain a license from the municipality in which he proposes to do business, and that he will have to make a substantial deposit with that municipality as a guarantee of his good faith. The local knowledge which is possessed by a municipality will enable the authorities to know whether the party is of good repute. We aim to prevent an irresponsible person establishing a private banking business and taking deposits, and then, by and by, having a disaster follow. We exempt from this certain cooperative and agricultural organizations, the character of which is well understood; but all these people who have been undertaking to receive large deposits and then involve depositors in heavy losses, will, we hope, be reached by the clause which we propose.
Those are the main provisions of the bill which I am presenting to the House. There are many minor things which I do not propose to mention now. Again, I want to say that I realize the fact that there are strong views held by many hon. members of this House and many citizens outside as regards the need of material changes in the Bank Act. I hope and believe that on a thorough inquiry such as that which will take place before the Committee on Banking and Commerce, some of the erroneous impressions regarding the present banking system will be removed. At all events, with the assurance of the desire of the government to have as full an inquiry as possible into the matter, I am going to ask hon. gentlemen to reserve their judgment until that inquiry takes place, and in the meantime to see their way clear to let this bill progress so that it may reach the committee on Banking and Commerce at any early date.

I entirely concur in the procedure outlined by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). There is no use in discussing this bill at present and in advance of the evidence. I think we shall serve our common purpose, which is to get the best results we can out of this bill, by letting the matter take the course which my hon.

friend now proposes, passing it through its initial stages and referring it at once to the committee on Banking and Commerce.

This resolution on which the bill is to be based, calls for the full ten-year period. The date as stated in the resolution is 1st July, 1933. It might appear in the course of the investigation that it would be better to have charters extended for less than the full ten years. If this resolution carries, would it be possible to make such a change?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The bill will propose the ordinary ten-year period; but there is no reason why the committee might not adopt a suggestion along the line of my hon. friend's proposal.
Sir liENRY DRAYTON: Or in any other direction.
