speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: Immigration and Colonization-immigration outside service-salaries, $700,000.

I do not intend to discuss the whole question of immigration at great length or in any general way, but I desire to direct a few remarks to the minister (Mr. Stewart) and to his colleagues on this very important subject. I am sure the House will have noted that the discussion which has taken place during the past week is receiving a great deal of public attention. It is generally recognized, I think, that the immigration policy of the government is a matter of primary importance to the country at large. My particular intention in rising to-day is to advise the minister and the government that in taking this important step which they propose in connection with their declared policy on immigration, they must do so with their eyes open. I should not like to sit silent in my seat and allow these estimates to pass and then next year, perhaps, find myself called upon to bring to the attention of the minister some of the results that might ensue from a policy of this character not in the best interests of the country. If I sat silent and allowed estimates to go through without any comment upon this important subject, the minister might well say afterwards that the hon. member having refrained from giving any expression of opinion, he was justified in regarding that silence as consent. In my estimation the bargain, or arrangement, or contract which the minister has entered into with the Canada Colonization Company is fraught with very grave possibilities. I think my hon. friend is entering upon a road that will lead him to possible chaos and perhaps even worse. I am not suggesting at this moment that there is any intent on the part of the minister or of those associated with him to commit any act of a dishonourable character, not at all; but what I do see in this bargain is, as I have stated, the danger of grave possibilities, and I want the minister to be fully apprised of my views on the subject, as also, I trust, the views of hon. gentlemen in the House generally.
Now, let us briefly examine this matter. The Canada Colonization Company has entered into an agreement or, as I choose to call it, a bargain, with the government. By virtue of that bargain, the government must accept, whether it does so in specific terms or not, the responsibility for the actions of the Canada Colonization Company, its agents and servants. And whether the government willingly accepts that responsibility or not, let the 4 p.m. committee be assured of this, that if anything does occur that is calculated to be an injury to any of the expected immigrants, or any other people of the community, the public will place the responsibility on the government after the difficulty or trouble is discovered. The minister himself stated that the Canada Colonization Company and the government had fully discussed this matter. He informed the House that several conferences had been held; and I find in a statement by the company itself, set forth in a very great detail in a full-page advertisement in a newspaper I have

.Supply-Immigration

under my hand, certain facts which I purpose bringing to the attention of the committee, so that hon. members may properly judge of their importance. For instance, there is a statement, which confirms what the minister says, that the whole project has been fully discussed with the government, with the minister, with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) with the hon. member for South Renfrew, minister without portfolio, (Mr. Low), and with a committee of the cabinet. I recite this merely to show that the matter has apparently been the subject of concurrence on the part of the government as a whole. The minister says that a committee of the cabinet "have had many conferences with the association." The statement of the Western Canada Colonization Association shows that the working capital of the company has been over-subscribed to the extent of $1,500,000. Why should they, under those conditions, find it necessary to receive from the government a grant of $40,000 and further sums at the rate of $10,000 a month for the purposes of carrying out their project? That is a pertinent query, and one in respect to which I think the committee should be furnished with the fullest possible information. The association claim also that their project has been approved by the imperial government, the Dominion government, and the Canadian railway companies-meaning by the latter, I presume, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways. If that is the case, do these three bodies share the liabilities of the colonization company? Are they jointly responsible? If so, in what way? Has the Imperial government definitely entered into this agreement? If it has, the documents showing to what extent they have accepted responsibility should be laid on the Table. The same applies to the railway companies; if they are equally liable we should know just to what extent that liability goes.
The next thing claimed by the association is that they expect to spend-I am quoting their own figures-$30,000,000 or $40,000,000 in the next five years. I want the committee to note this fact, because it is evidence of the enormous scope of this movement. To what extent has the government, which is a party to the association's activities, supervision or control, in sight or knowledge, of the expenditure of this large amount within five or ten years? That is another query that should be fully and satisfactorily answered to-day. The chief reason why I at least am a little alarmed about this part of the agreement is because the association states that the major portion of this $30,000,000 or $40,-

000,000 will be expended on commissions. The significance of that will be better understood if I point out to the House the nature of those commissions. In a full-page advertisement the association declare that they are securing in the United States and other countries efficient real estate agents to push the sale of Canadian lands. I will quote the minister at this point. He says, page 1148 of unrevised Hansard of this session:
They-
That is, the association.
-have in the United States to-day sixty agents who are operating on a commission basis, who receive for their service something like ten per cent per acre.
I am not questioning the bona fides of this association, but here is a body with which the Dominion government is closely identified, which has in the United States what are known among real estate men as high pressure salesmen, out selling Canadian lands on behalf of the Canadian government and this association, and receiving a commission, of ten per cent. When you turn loose an accomplished real estate agent who has in view the possibility of a ten per cent commission, his main object is to make as much as possible- to earn the commission, no matter how he earns it. He will tell any story that he can "get by" with in order to earn that commission. I want the government to appreciate that point. Has the minister any supervision over these agents from the United States? So far as I can discover, he has none whatever. Does the minister know the names of these "sixty agents"-I quote his own words

"who are operating" in the United States to-day? Does he know their bona fides, their qualifications, their trustworthiness? Or is it not reasonable to assume that this great army of agents, which will multiply very largely as business proceeds, are not known to the government at all? On the face of it we must conclude that the government is wholly ignorant of the detailed administration of the association. But the government must be prepared to assume responsibility for the activities of these agents. My experience- which is not inconsiderable

in connection with salesmen who are working on a commission basis is that even though they intend to be honest, they very frequently, if not almost generally, overdraw the picture and seek to earn the commission rather than give accurate information. At the rate of 200 families a year, $10,000 a month for ten months means a cost to the government of $500 per family. If any figure of that kind is to be paid by the government for these settlers, the country

Supply-Immigration
will be put to a very large expenditure indeed. I strongly advise the government against the expenditure of large sums of public money for the importation of immigrants. I do not think an examination of the records respecting immigration will encourage the minister very much from that point of view. The Atlantic Trading Company, for instance, and other institutions of that kind, the movement of the Doukhobors to western Canada, and such like, where there was encouragement, bargaining, or any assistance given, rarely resulted in any benefit to the country.
Let me take another point. Under this agreement, according to the minister's statement, and verified again by this full-page advertisement, it is purposed to arrange for 32-year agreements of sale with the intending settler, and an illustration is given in the advertisement to this effect. Take a 160-acre farm at $20 an acre; that would cost $3,200. The cash payment asked is $320-I want the committee to follow this bit of information. There is an agreement made for $2,880, and under the scale of payments set forth in this advertisement, and referred to by the minister himself in his speech, at the end of ten years the settler would still owe $2,883, or more than the face value of the agreement when he started out. But that is not all. What becomes of the $320 of cash payment? The whole of that $320 goes into commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would like to understand how my hon. friend arrives at that figure, that the amount would be $2,883 at the end of ten years.

I have the statement
worked out here on an actuarial basis by this company. The first year it is $2,880. There is a $320 cash payment, which, deducted from $3,200, leaves $2,880. I will not read the figures for each year, but will take one or two at random. The first year the principal balance is $2,880; the sixth year there is still owing a balance of $3,095.71; the tenth year it is $2,883.15; the twelfth year $2,756.77, and so you go on down till in the twentieth year it is $2,074. In the thirty-second year the principal is wiped out with the final payment, but for the first three years no payment is made at all, and the interest is added to the principal and it takes up to the tenth year for the purchaser to catch up what he has lost in the added interest in that period. So the statement I make is quite correct that at the end of ten years the settler still owes $2,883.15.
What I wish to draw attention to is that the minister has apparently accepted the scheme. He is so quoted here, and has so stated him-
84J
self, and I am pointing out that this is not a very satisfactory agreement. Although the 32-year payment scheme sounds all right, if you say it quick and do not examine it too closely, you find when you come to examine it closely, that there is very little advantage to the settler in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is exactly the same as any other amortization scheme of that character. It is no different. There is nothing new.
I quite agree but I am pointing out what the result is.
The hon. member argues that at the end of three years these conditions readily lend themselves to a man leaving the organization?

Certainly. I have a few more observations to make in regard to this bargain. I am trying to give to the committee the facts. What becomes of the $329 cash payment?
And this presents to my mind what is really an absurdity. The $320 goes to the Colonization Company, and not to the vendor. Here is where the vendor receives a blank cheque, as it were. The vendor who is asked in this advertisement to list his property with 'the government, and who must enter into an agreement for five years gets nothing at all. He cannot get anything at all for some three or four years, and then he receives at the end of the three years $40.80 out of this liability of $3,200. The first $320 cash payment goes to these high-pressure salesmen. It goes through the association to their agents. They are paying to their agents in the United States and elsewhere ten per cent, or something like that, but it all goes to the association. The vendor gets nothing at all. Does the minister think for a moment that the vendors of these properties who are expected to come under this scheme will permit a condition of that kind? According to this advertisement, there is a very clever inducement held out to vendors to list their properties, and it is this, that the Imperial government, the Canadian government, and the railway companies are behind this scheme. Now the average person with property to sell will say: They are the people to whom I should entrust my property. But they will wake up very shortly to the fact that they are getting little or nothing out of their property. The association deducts one per cent of the six per cent interest in addition to the $320, and that lasts for eight
Supply-Immigration

years. That is another very extraordinary charge. Then we go further. The Dominion government have certain responsibilities.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Is not that one per cent for the purpose of acting as agent for the vendor, if they so act?
Quite so, but what I am getting at is the unsatisfactory nature of this so-called agreement. The association get one per cent of the interest, leaving five per cent to the vendor.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In the event of their continuing to act as agents. If they do not they get nothing.
Oh, certainly, but the object of my hon. friend's bargain and the expenditure of public money is that the thing is going to be a success.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I will discuss that later. What I want my hon. friend to point out to the committee, if he will do it-and I am quite certain he wants to make a fair presentation-is this, that if they act as agents for the vendor for whom they have sold the land, for that service they will get one per cent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Of the money they collect?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

No, one per cent of the six per cent interest. That is where the purchaser pays six per cent per annum, the association acting as agent for eight years, following the three years where no payment is made, and it is allowed to take one of the six per cent paid in interest. That is its charge for acting as agent. I want to say to the minister that that arrangement will fail, and I think it will fail in two ways. First, I think it is simply inviting trouble and disappointment for those who purchase under this scheme, and secondly, I am certain that once the vendors realize-what shall I say?-the shabbiness of it, and I do not use the word offensively, as far as their interests are concerned, they will withdraw their property unless they become involved for five years before they properly understand the conditions. I think my hon. friend is simply laying up a peck of trouble, if I might use that expression.
Now then, what about the government? The government are asked not only to assume a vast responsibility as to this association's activities, but they must extend and maintain agencies in all countries of the world, or virtually so,-that is to maintain and extend agencies in the United States, 
in Europe, and in Great Britain at the expense of this country, and for which we are being asked to-day to vote some million-odd dollars. In addition to that the government, not only gives to this association these enormous and valuable privileges and its whole moral support-and I believe actual responsibility-must pay for the advertising, must carry on an effective advertising campaign. I would think that out of the ten per cent or twenty per cent that this concern get they might at least pay for the expense of maintaining agencies and the expense of advertising and publicity. But no: the government pay that in addition to its grants and its gifts to this association.
Now, I want to read to the committee what appears to me to give a fair interpretation of the meaning of this whole scheme. At the bottom of this full-page ad of the association are these words in leaded type: Owners of vacant agricultural land within 15 miles of railways in the western provinces are requested to list their properties immediately with the Canada Colonization Association, Bank of Hamilton Building, Winnipeg.
That seems to be really what is at the bottom of the whole business. Here is a magnificient opportunity for this Canada Colonization Company to induce people to list their property with them, and, if they did list, they would be bound for five years; their property would be listed with the company for that period of time. Is it fair- I put it to the minister very frankly- to use the name of the Imperial government, associated with the Dominion government and the big railway companies of Canada to induce property holders to list their property with these agents? I do not think it is. Because, after all, these people-I care not how estimable they may be as citizens- are nothing more or less than a real estate association. You cannot escape that point-, there is no escape from it. Their whole activity is based upon the very revenue that they expect to derive from the sale of lands; -it is on a commission basis, they pay their agents on a commission basis just the same as any land company does. My hon. friend referred to the general manager in quite glowing terms and his qualification, quoted by the minister was that he was the successful manager of the Luseland Company. Now, this is the point I want to warn the government and the House against. Not that these people are not honest or honourable, not at all, but that the whole proposition is largely a real estate listing and sale proposition, and the government is entering into that rather

Supply-Immigration
than into an immigration policy. That is what I want to warn the government against.
Now, to summarize the situation very briefly, we have these facts: The government subsidizes this company to the extent of $100,000 annually; the government is to maintain its offices all over the world at the cost of the public treasury of Canada; the government is to pay for the advertising, or to maintain the advertising; and must turn over all their emigration machinery to the use of this association; every move made by the association, in so far as this scheme is concerned, must be supplemented by the organization of the Immigration department. And the association is to get ten per cent on the sale price, plus the one per cent interest for ten years. The association employs the agents, the government does not employ them; and the association alone controls the agents, the government does not control them. I doubt if the minister has any idea of the extent of the provision with respect to these agents. I feel very much alarmed about this point in particular: the turning loose of agents in all quarters of the world. And with what guarantee? Simply this: Go out and sell Canadian western lands: the Dominion government is behind you: this association- with the backing of the Dominion and the Imperial governments-is behind you; and you will get ten per cent in respect of any lands you sell upon which immigrants enter. That means, the agents will be telling pretty roseate stories. My hon. friends to my left have been telling us some very doleful stories. I am not altogether agreeing with them, although there is much in what they have said; but it would be the height of folly for this government to associate themselves with the high-pressure salesman's story as to the conditions that obtain in the Canadian West. Most of them-certainly ninety per cent of them-have never seen the Canadian West I venture to say.
I now wish to reiterate what I said a moment ago. In fact., my purpose in rising to-day is to press home upon the government that they must be prepared to accept full responsibility for whatever results may come from this campaign.
Let me say just a few words more before I take my seat. It is not to my mind so much a question of immigration; the problem is one of emigration. That is not a new statement, I merely reiterate what others have said. I think my hon. friend the minister would be well advised to turn to his colleagues and put some very pertinent questions to them. My hon. friend is the Acting Minister of Immigration and Colonization.
It appears, to me at least, that he has separated himself and his department from the government. He is going Qut with this colonization scheme, and other measures, to carry on an immigration policy and he has ignored the fact, apparently, that there are some sound reasons for the emigration from Canada of so many people during this past year or two. Why does he not tell the Minister of Finance that one of the reasons why people are leaving Canada, one of the reasons why there is such hard times in the industrial world, is because of heavy taxation? and in some regards, as I have stated before to the House this session, unfair taxation. This is not an attack I am making upon the Minister of Finance, I am simply stating what I think to be a problem-a problem that ought to be faced before we enter into any extensive scheme of immigration. Stop this emigration before dealing with this problem. I invite him. therefore, to bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance, who ought to co-operate with him in this matter, the necessity of meeting this problem of taxation, solving it-simplifying it if you like to use that term-so as to promote industrial activity and more contentment in the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
include customs duties in that "heavy taxation?"

I felt sure that question
would be put, but I hardly expected the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) to ask it; I really expected it to come from hon. gentlemen to my left. I do not wish, nor do I purpose, being side-tracked into a discussion of the tariff policy. My opinions on the tariff question are well known. The problem that I am. propounding-namely dealing with the financial situation as regards industry and agriculture-is the responsibility of the Minister of Finance and not mine. I am prepared at the proper time-and when it comes in a few weeks I shall avail myself of the opportunity-to state my opinions very clearly and I shall have no hesitancy in doing so. But I say that is the problem to be dealt with; and the minister, before entering into this scheme, ought to have addressed himself to' the Minister of Finance, in regard to it. He should also have addressed himself to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and asked him to co-operate in the promotion of trade. I know he has done something, I know he wants to do something; but it is only by the co-ordinated activity of the government that these things can be done, and not by one minister framing a policy for his department alone.
Supply-Immigration

It would appear to me as if the ministry were all at sixes and sevens, and not co-operating at all. Referring to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), upon his shoulders, as the head of the Agricultural department of Canada, rests the responsibility of solving or leading in the solution, of the problem of why agriculture is not successful to-day. I do not say he is responsible for the problem, but I say he is responsible for its solution, or for the lead in attempted solution. My hon. friend (Mr. Stewart, Argenteuil) should have addressed himself to the Minister of Agriculture before he propounded this policy, which, I am certain in my mind, will bring nothing but pain, suffering, disappointment and discord. My hon. friend has the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to fall back upon. It is true that he stated the other day that the Prime Minister was consulted in the matter. To my mind at least, there is little evidence that this scheme were properly considered by the government as a whole. It might have been, but if it was, then it reflects but little credit on the government. My hon. friend for Fort William (Mr. Manion) the other day made a very excellent suggestion to this House. He made an excellent speech, and he made a reference that merits the closest consideration of the government, and I hope it will receive such consideration. One of the great difficulties in Canada is a thousand-mile gap between eastern and western Canada. It is a geographical difficulty, but the fact is that a barren, almost depopulated, or unpopulated, area exists and while it may not be caused by the government, yet I believe the first responsibility of a settlement scheme in Canada should be towards bringing the eastern part of Canada together with the west. There you have a wide .barren territory, with no traffic developing or little traffic, very little settlement, and with a lot of splendid land, and it would behoove the minister, I think, in co-operation with the Ontario government, to study how he could populate that hinterland of Ontario, or that gap between the East and the West. The speech of the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) the other day was one of the best expositions of this problem given in the House this session. He referred in a different way altogether to this same problem which my hon. friend for Fort William mentioned. Here you have an hon. member from Ontario and an hon. member from Manitoba, both recognizing that the difficulty was to bring the population in their respective districts, bordering on this gap to which I have referred, to a level commensurate with means that exist there 
to sustain a large population. Therefore, I say to the minister if he wants to inaugurate a first-rate, a fundamentally sound, scheme of immigration, there is where he can find scope for his activities. Why should he at this moment seek to force, through high-pressure land salesmen-I want the minister to get that-upon the three prairie provinces, whose representatives in this House tell us there is no use putting more settlers there at the present time because of the difficulties they are placed in-why should he force this immigration? Why should he, through the high-pressure salesman and through this scheme, force immigration into the provinces, when we know perfectly well that in northern Ontario there is just as fine opportunity for a different type of agriculture, but for agriculture waiting for assistance? I would certainly be more than willing to vote money direct to assistance of settlers in that area, rather than to vote money to be expended in connection with this enormous, and, I think, highly painted visionary scheme, presented to the minister by the Canada Colonization Association, and accepted by him.
I rose for the purpose of impressing, if I could, upon the minister and the government, the dangers that confront them and the government, the parliament and the country in the acceptance of this contract. I fear the minister has made a serious mistake, and I do not think it is too late now to retreat from the position in which he finds himself. It is true that this project was precipitated some time last fall, and there may have been negotiations carried on some time since, but parliament has not yet approved of it. I would not want to be one who would say to the government " we must resist absolutely your policy in immigration ", I have grave doubts about it and serious apprehensions as to its effect, and I want the minister, if. he persists in going on, to realize that these dangerous waters lie ahead of him and what the results may be; so that he cannot come back to parliament next year and say that parliament as a whole participated in the scheme.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think it appropriate that at this moment I should give the committee some information with respect to the organization in regard to which my hon. friend for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) has just offered his criticisms. The Canada Colonization Association is not a new organization and was not a new organization when this government took office. It had the endorsation of the government which preceded this government through their Minis-

Supply-Immigration
ter of Agriculture. It has been in existence for some two or three years to my certain knowledge. I do not desire to cover that ground, but I want to point out to the committee that in the very difficult situation in which I found myself with respect to this question of immigration, I felt that this organization, patriotic as they called themselves, which my hon. friend denies this afternoon-
I do not deny it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the hon. member does not deny it directly he denies it by implication.
I made no such statement. I said I did not question the bona fides of the association, I am not in a position to do so. Next year we may be in that position.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Nor is it my intention to give a certificate of character to these men, but simply, if I can, to place my position before this committee.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The hon. minister referred to the former government having approved of the organization-I think he used the word "approved." I hope he does not mean to imply that the former government in any way approved of any plan by which this organization would get any advantages or any special assistance from the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I was not inferring that a letter had been given them by the Minister of Immigration, and in fairness to him I need not deal with some changes that have transpired since the occasion of that letter. This organization was started some three years ago. I well remember the propaganda carried on throughout Canada. It was heralded as a patriotic endeavour on the part of the citizens to settle privately-owned lands along our existing railways. I mentioned the other day they had difficulty about their land listing proposition, inasmuch as they were asking for legislation to validate listing over a period of two years, if I remember the circumstances properly. At that time, as Premier of the province of Alberta, I refused that, and I have had some personal experience in land selling and the dealing in land, and one of the very practical difficulties that a Minister of Immigration or any government is faced with in connection with immigration to-day is that we have no longer available, within reasonable distance of our railways, land that we can offer freely to attract settlement to Canada. That was the great lure in the past;
but although there are millions of acres of land still available, we cannot advise people to go into outlying areas and to take up land for themselves, as they did formerly when coming to Canada.
May I ask the minister a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will let me make my statement this afternoon, I shall be glad to answer all questions that anyone may wish to ask at a later date.
That is the situation we have to face. I said the other day, and I repeat, that we must have our propaganda, our advertising and our discussion confined very largely to encouraging incoming settlement amongst agricultural classes. There can be no doubt about that. There is at the moment undoubtedly a place for people in Canada within the boundaries of our urban centres, and that is becoming more apparent every day. The organization we have at the moment throughout Canada would indicate that there will be a fairly lively demand for mechanics to engage in the building trades in the various cities of Canada, and we are ready, willing and glad to make that known in countries from which we hope to attract settlers. But when I mention the great railway problem and the difficulty that has been mentioned by my hon. friend, namely, the burden of taxation that is bearing down upon the shoulders of the people of Canada, one way in which this can be relieved is by getting additional people into this country. That is not the only way, it is true, but that is one of the ways. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) stated the other day -that one of the lures we were offering to people to come to Canada was to come and assist us with our very heavy burden. Let me answer my hon. friend in two ways. We are not overpersuading people in the countries from which we hope to attract settlers, and there is no difficulty about convincing them that their opportunity in Canada is better than in the country in which they are living to-day. I am speaking of people engaged in agriculture in those countries, and I speak of Great Britain, Scandinavia, the European ; continent and the United States. Therefore, I think we can say with caution and safety, that we are offering a better opportunity, if we confiine that settlement within reasonable distance of railway facilities. Thus, we are not asking them to come to Canada, primarily to assist us in carrying our burden. If I thought we were doing that, I would be the last one to advo-
Supply-Immigration

cate that our agents scattered throughout the various countries I have mentioned, should offer the advantages of Canada to incoming settlers. Moreover, I have been very careful, in discussion with agents at Chicago, with Colonel Smith, who is in charge of twelve agencies in Great Britain, and with Mr. Willans, who has recently gone to the Continent, to ask them to be sure not to over-advertise, and not to overpersuade-if that is the proper way to put the matter-people to come to this country, but to offer the advantages that Canada is ready to offer, to all who intend leaving countries in which we are engaged in settlement work to-day. I hope that answers some of the questions raised by some hon. members with respect to the propaganda that we are carrying on. First, it is to the advantage of these people to come, because I believe they can better their condition. Second, they can undoubtedly-no one will deny the fact- be of a great deal of assistance to the people of Canada.
As regards migration, as near as I can discover, that has been going on since 1885 in greater or less degree. That ii has gone on during the last year, no one will deny, and probably to a somewhat greater degree than on former occasions; but the unprecedented prosperity in urban centres of the United States has been the attraction. Whether that will continue is problematical; but at all events, I am getting assurances from the agencies of the United States that a very considerable movement wall come to Canada this year.
As regards the Canada Colonization Association when they first approached me, they were endorsed by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, by the Canadian National Railway Company, by the banking institutions of Canada, and by boards of trade from one end of the country to the other. And let me say to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) that those institutions, those boards of trade and those individuals who lent their endorsation to this scheme, did so on the scheme outlined by my hon. friend this afternoon. That was the scheme that was endorsed almost universally, as I stated the other day, from Montreal to the Pacific coast.
Do these railway companies, boards of trade and banking institutions accept any responsibility for the results of the activities of this company?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is another question. I will come to that later on. I simply want to state this afternoon that,

as Minister of Immigration, I felt that this organization had the backing of the people of Canada who were anxious about land settlement. I do not propose to discuss at any length this afternoon the question of the basis of settlement, or the scheme outlined so well by my hon. friend. Responsible organizations in Canada have stated both publicly and privately that immigration is the great question in this country. I say that it is one of them, and I have repeatedly said that, it is, perhaps, not the greatest one, because some of my hon. friends who are sitting across the floor of this House and many on this side will, I am sure, agree with me, that many other things could be done that would, perhaps assist the situation. I have great respect for the opinion of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). I think, perhaps, something might be done by way of tariff reduction that would help the situation materially. But, while I say that, let me say that I cannot forget that there is upon the shoulders of this government the responsibility of raising a tremendous sum of money annually, and the thing that the Immigration department could best advertise would be the fact that we have at last reached a point where our revenue covers our expenditure. I am not unmindful of these facts. As I say, I have a great deal of respect for my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) who has to deal with matters of this kind, and I am prepared to support him when he has to take into consideration the situation as it exists throughout Canada. My hon. friend for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) had a different idea from mine altogether; and throughout Canada different views are held. But I say that the one paramount thing we must consider, the one question we have to face at all times, is how we shall raise the revenue. My hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) said-and I am not going to say anything on that point-that it was the method of raising this revenue that he objected to. Undoubtedly, his view in regard to this matter is different from mine. Now, I do not believe that it is within the province of a government to go into the real estate business; and I want to keep as far away from it as does my hon. friend for Vancouver Centre. I do not want to see the government of Canada implicated in any scheme in which it has to act as agent between the vendor and the purchaser of land. Indeed, I do not believe that the government could ever occupy that position, either through the agency of the Soldier Settlement Board or of any other organization that might be in its direct pay. My hon. friend

Supply-Immigration
may say that because we are offering to assist this organization, which is backed by the money of private interests and private individuals throughout Canada and which has the endorsation of all the people and all the responsible bodies I have mentioned, that we are nevertheless making a serious mistake. Well, I think that you, Mr. Chairman, as well as other members of this committee, so far as this debate has progressed, will agree with me that the man who could evolve an immigration policy that would satisfy all the members of this House would be a second Moses.	*
Greater than Moses.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Possibly.
That, at any rate, is my opinion, and I form that opinion after listening to the speeches of hon. gentlemen on all sides of this House. It is a fair assumption, I think, that the members of parliament are representative of the feelings of the people throughout Canada. And whatever our views may be, I think there is one thing about which we are all agreed, and that is that we must get people into Canada. I say, therefore, let us bring into the country people who have a fair chance of making a success. My hon. friend says that we should have a well rounded out policy and should beware of the difficulties that beset us. I said the other day that I was aware of the conflicting opinions throughout Canada; which I had heard from all quarters; and I am well aware also of the difficulties under which the agricultural population of Canada is labouring. But I still think that there is an opportunity for saving the situation and giving a decent chance to the people who come amongst us. Let me repeat again, most emphatically, that if I did not feel that way I should not be advocating immigration to this country.
My hon. friend makes the statement that this organization may get the government of Canada into difficulties. Now, I said the other day, and I want in all fairness to repeat, that from what I know about the organization it has not the entire approval of all the people who have subscribed their money to it; that is, I mean, the scheme under which this organization is operating at the present moment. And when I make that statement I want to deal with the objection that has been voiced in reference to this matter. I stated that the Canadian Pacific Railway lent their endorsation to the scheme, and when I spoke of the scheme I meant the 32-year plan of land selling. Colonel J. S. Dennis, who is a strong advocate of the scheme which my hon. friend has criticized, as it affects
the vendor and the purchaser, does however object-and in fairness to him I make the statement-to the taking of the ten per cent commission by the organization; and that is one of the reasons why he to-day is not an advocate of this particular scheme. He does not approve of the taking of that commission. But let me explain.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I understood the minister to say that the scheme had the approval of the late government and also of the various institutions to which he has referred; and his latest interjection raises that very question. What scheme was it that had their approval? Was it the scheme now before the people, or some previous scheme? I hold in my hand an early prospectus of the company, and there have been no fewer than three variations in it since last September. One important variation, and one that has prompted me to rise now and interrupt the minister, is the very point of commission. The prospectus I have in my hand, and which I am given to understand was issued about September last, with two variations since, provides a commission of fifty cents an acre on the land actually sold. Taking the illustration which appears in this flaring advertisement referred to by my hon. friend for Vancouver Centre, we find that 160 acres rated at $20 per acre produce a commission, not of $80 as would be the case on a fifty-cent basis, but of $320. And the same thing would apply to the sale 5 p.m. of the whole 900,000 acres if the same basis were adopted. What I want to ask the minister is this: Is he in a position to say that the gentleman he has referred to as the late president-in fact, he was the only president-Sir John Willison, who presided for a period of three months, did approve of the fifty cents an acre commission or the ten per cent commission, which is very much larger? There are many other features on which I should like information from the minister, but for the moment I will confine my question to this point.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Sir John Willison did approve of the scheme. He toured the western provinces and spoke to the boards of trade. I may say that he also addressed the Board of Trade in Toronto and outlined the very scheme my hon. friend has discussed this afternoon.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The ten per cent commission?

What scheme?
Mr. STEWART .Argenteuil): The scheme you outlined this afternoon.
Supply-I mmigra tion
The ten per cent, commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, the
scheme as it is outlined in the advertisement referred to by my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: There are three variations in it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Well, let us deal with the last one, because we shall only become entangled if we try to consider them all simultaneously. I will confine my remarks to the last scheme and try to give the committee a fair statement of the facts as they exist in connection with this matter. Colonel J. S. Dennis makes the statement that this organization was to be patriotic, to be supported entirely by private subscription. It was not to take any commission but was to be supported and paid altogether out of the moneys to be raised by the various subscribers to the organization. Now, I want to be perfectly fair and to make myself clear on the matter.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Was not that the proposition that Sir John Willison lent himself to? In other words, did he not advocate a scheme that was to be patriotic, a philanthropic proposition. I am told that these gentlemen did subscribe $1',000,000, but that there was no real estate proposition for commission at all. They were to devote the money for a period of probably three years to the encouragement of the work of settlement, and when that was done, it was supposed that the company would carry itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: With the single exception of Colonel J. S. Dennis I do not know of, nor has there come to my knowledge, any other objector. And I presume that Colonel J. S. Dennis was speaking on behalf of the Canadian Pacific Railway. In fairness to Mr. Beatty I may say that several conversations took place between him and myself with respect to this matter prior to the visit to Great Britain of Mr. Brown and his associates to interest the overseas government. I had been pressed ever since July of last year to lend assistance to this organization on the ground that it would be in the best interests of the settlement of these privately-owned lands-in other words, the getting of these lands out of the hands of owners who could not utilize them and were not cultivating them.
Does the minister know why General McRae left this organization?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes,-well, perhaps I should not say that. I do not know why he left, but I do know that his scheme was not acceptable to the board of directors.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Was his salary not fixed at $25,000 a year?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no knowledge of that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I am informed on an authority which I do not dispute for a moment that for acting as president he was to receive $25,000 -and that in connection with a scheme which had been started for patriotic and philanthropic purposes. I understand that that was a source of dissatisfaction.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The only knowledge I have of the organization during the presidency of General McRae was when he asked me for legislation in Alberta to make compulsory the listing of privately owned lands. I do not know what salary he was paid or how long he was employed by this organization.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I am not saying he was paid that, but I know that amount was fixed, and I am given to understand there was trouble over it. One does not wonder that there was.
The minister refers to Colonel Dennis, of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Do the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Canadian National Railways officially endorse this scheme?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Let me
make a differentiation to my hon. friend. So far as the 32-year plan of land settlement is concerned, yes-all of them agree.
And the ten per cent to the company?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No. I have tried to point out that Colonel Dennis objected to that provision for the ten per cent to go to the company. An organization of this kind appeals to the Canadian Pacific Railway; they think it is in the best interests of Canada and that it ought to be supported by the government; and they are a unit in expressing approval. Now, have I made that plain to my hon. friend? So far as the purpose of this organization is to settle these lands, it has received entire approval. The one difficulty is the objection to the ten per cent taken by the company.
I have stated that pressure was being exerted from all quarters in this matter, and that criticism was being made of the government and of the Immigration department in that they were not participating in the overseas scheme. It has been stated that we are urged largely by the transportation companies to bring settlers into Canada. That is

Supply-Immigration
not the ease; I will deal with that in a moment or two, in connection with our propaganda for getting settlement. But I yielded to the extent of assisting this organization as we did last fall. They went forward; they listed in the neighbourhood of half a million acres of land. I cannot of course, take an affidavit on this floor that the vendor of these lands knows all about the provisions of the listing; I assume he does. I have heard those who own land privately, private individuals as well as corporations, maligned because of the very fact that they were holding it. As one who had something to do with taxation I endeavoured in the province from which I come to make it unprofitable for the absentee landholder or the owner of land out of use to continue to hold that land. We imposed an unearned increment tax and we gave to those who improved their land a reduction of 25 per cent from the rate applying to unimproved areas so far as local taxation went. There is no property tax in that province, so that the man who holds unimproved land is more than walling to sell it. The greatest criticism I received from our agents was that there was no responsible organization to which we could send prospective settlers to purchase land. I have pointed out that I did not think it was good business for the government to go into a land selling scheme. For these reasons I thought it wise to utilize this organization to a certain extent in our scheme of settling those lands. I hold in my hand a telegram from Sir John Willison sent to me on September 30. It is to this effect:
Have just completed tour of West. Have had conferences with four western governments and with grain growers and held many public meetings. Interviews with all governments most satisfactory.
He interviewed the western governments and placed this scheme before them. The telegram continues:
All meetings warmly sympathetic. At Winnipeg meeting five hundred representative citizens called by James Stewart adopted with enthusiasm resolution offering plan Canada Colonization Association. Everywhere we emphasized action government in uniting all forces for immigration and settlement. Beatty has appointed Col Dennis to represent Canadian Pacific on operating committee association, and Chipman of Grain Growers Guide with approval Crerar has agreed represent western farmers.
May I ask whether any farmer's organizations in any part of Canada have endorsed this scheme?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Not to my knowledge, except that there is on record a letter from the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) endorsing it. In fairness to him I may say that except so far as this telegram
goes I did not know what connection we had with the organization at that time. But that propaganda, if you call it such, that settlement outlined by my hon. friend, was then in existence and it was on that basis that this enthusiastic reception was extended. That is what I want to convey to my hon. friend, because I am being severely criticized in connection with this matter.
I sometimes wonder, Mr. Chairman, whether if I had turned this thing down I would not have been criticized just as severely by some hon. gentlemen of this House for refusing assistance to this organization. I realize full well the difficulties of a position of this character. I want to do the best I can for the people of this country. My business is to get people into this country, and to bring them honestly and legitimately if it is humanly possible so to do, to bring in citizens who will assimilate with the life of this country and assist in nation-building here, no matter whether I am here as minister or whether this government or some other government is in existence. I have endeavoured to do this in a careful, conscientious way.
As I stated the other day, one other factor in inducing me to listen to the proposal of this organization was the fact that I knew of the activities of Mr. Howard Everett. I have known of his activities for years. Does anyone in this House, does anyone in this parliament think that the activities of governmental agencies alone in Canada have brought all the settlers in this country? Let me ask my hon. friends who have lived in western Canada, some of them longer than I have, do they not think that in a very large way the settlement that is in western Canada to-day was brought in by men who came in and purchased cheap land, and then went out and spent money and sold it and placed settlers on those lands? I frankly admit that some of them did not always tell the truth, that they over-coloured the picture, because as my hon. friend has rightly said, there is always an inducement to do that kind of thing. But here is one organization, and I would ask any hon. gentleman representing the areas that this company operated in for twenty years in Saskatchewan and central Alberta, have they heard any complaints about it? So far, as I am concerned, I have never heard that Howard Everett or his company misrepresented land to any individual whom they settled, but I have heard this, that where dissatisfaction existed they made it their business to change the individual to more congenial surroundings, and perhaps to better land, believing, and I think it is good business, that
Supply-Immigration

to have a satisfied settler was a better advertisement for them than to make the small sum of money that might accrue from refusing to make that exchange.
Mr. Chairman, I am not unmindful of the difficulties that surround a situation such as this, but I have felt that as one of the agencies for settlement we might give this organization a trial, and I have recommended it to the government. My hon. friend has said that there is a signed agreement in existence-perhaps I should qualify that statement that there would be a signed agreement in existence. There is not. We have discussed this matter from time to time, and undoubtedly this organization have certain promises of mine that I hold more or less in respect. I believe from the experience that I have had in connection with western Canada that this organization can be a real factor in settling western Canada, and that is the reason I am asking for the consideration of this committee.
My hon. friend made one other statement, that the agents of the government are to act with this company's agents. That is not the case. Rather is it the reverse. They are to carry on their own work. True, if you pick up an advertisement of our government in the United States you will find reference in one particular to this organization, namely, that they are in Canada and that we think it is an organization upon which the intending settler can depend for information of a reliable character, but he is under no obligation to purchase from the company. Furthermore, they .have not gone into Great Britain. They will confine their operations entirely to the United States. They will not even be in the eastern states. Their business, so far as this year at all events is concerned, will be bringing settlers from the western states to settle in western Canada, and I think that that is a task for which Mr. Everett is eminently fitted.
Our own immigration agents in the United States are working along the very same lines on which they have always worked. They are advertising Canada to the man who is intending to leave the United States and come here and settle, and I take it that there is no criticism of that. What I want to emphasize here and now is that the statement made the other day that we are endeavouring to bring people to Canada by false representation has not one tittle of foundation in fact. That is not true of our efforts in any country in the world, none excepted. We are endeavouring to advertise Canada as Canada exists, and the opportunities that are in this
'Mr. Chas. Stewart.]
country for those who are desirous to come here.
Let me follow that one step further and say this:	We do not approach any individual
until he has first made application to the agent. In the United States, for example, where advertisements are carried in the newspapers, when we get an application for information from some individual a card is sent out asking him for certain information, which is filed when it comes back. A mark is made upon the map indicating where this individual lives, and he is invited to meet on a certain day one of our agents who will be at some convenient point to which he can drive in. He then interviews the agent and the advantages of Canada are placed before him, the conditions are depicted just as they exist. If he is interested, we hope to get him to come up to Canada. That is true of the American field, and true also of the English field except that we go into it a little more intensively over there. I had hoped this year to have a number of motor cars in Great Britain. We have one in the British field at the moment, and we hope to have two or three carrying advertisements and showing motion pictures and giving lectures on the advantages of this country. We have very strong competitors in the Old Land. The Australian government and the South African government are all in the field in the Old Land for immigration. One of the principal difficulties in connection with moving people from the Old Land to Canada is that a great many of those who are willing to come and would make very desirable settlers are financially unable to make the move; but I do not want to be led away into a discussion of that phase at the moment.
I welcome criticism from any hon. member of this House. I am not averse to it at all. My object is to recommend to the government, in the light of this discussion and the various suggestions that are offered by members of this House, what is the best thing to do under the circumstances, what will be in the best interests of the country in connection with immigration.
One hon. member the other day asked me to give him the personnel of this organization. I have the names here, but before giving them I had perhaps better say a word or two about Sir John Willison. Sir John Willison was in charge of this organization for a short space of time. I have said that he endorsed the scheme that has been presented to the committee by my hon. friend this afternoon, that he has retired, and that the reason for his retirement was a difference of opinion that

Supply-Immigration
apparently existed between some supporters of the organization here in the East and its vice president. In addition he pointed out to me that he does not feel that he understands all the ramifications of an organization of this kind; he feels that he cannot give his time to it, and that he is not warranted in taking a salary for devoting attention to an organization whose work he does not thoroughly understand. That is the purport of his statement with respect to this matter. I have said to the committee that I believe the success of this organization depends upon Mr. Howard Everett. I do not believe it depends upon Mr. Brown because Mr. Brown, with all due respect to him, has had little or no experience in the actual selling or disposing of lands. He has, no doubt, been valuable in stirring up public opinion and getting the subscriptions of those organizations that have backed this institution so far-and many of them are backing it to-day.
Let me read to you the names of the gentlemen who are in control of this association, although I think I shall have to make an exception in the case of my hon. friend the leader of the Progressives (Mr. Forke) whose name appears here. My .hon. friend, however, made an explanation the other day with respect to his connection with the association, and I do not know that there is anything I can add to his statement.
I am not at all ashamed to be in the association.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No. I want to give the committee all the information with respect to this matter that I am in possession of, and to be fair to all parties concerned. The officers and directors of the company are:
Vice-President, M. A. Brown.
General Manager, Howard Everett.
Secretary-Treasurer, F. D. L. Smith.
Directors:-
M. A. Brown, Winnipeg.
W. W. Evans, Winnipeg.
Robert Forke, Pipestone, Man.
Col. F. J. James, Regina, Sask.
S. W. Johns, Saskatoon, Sask.
J. F. Cairns, Saskatoon, Sask.
J. K. R. Williams, Regina, Sask.
Sam McLeod, Prince Albert, Sask.
Chas. McDonald, M.L.A., Prince Albert, Sask.
Hon. R. G. Brett, (Governor of Alberta), Edmonton.
Pat. Burns, Calgary, Alberta.
.. C. S. Noble, Nobleford, Alberta.
Brig. Gen. H. F. McDonald, Vancouver, B.C.
Col. Nelson Spencer, Vancouver, B.C.
Eastern Advisory Board:-
A. M. MacQueen, Toronto, Ont.
Robert Hobson, Hamilton, Ont.
Frank Cockshutt, Brantford, Ont.
Lt. Col. R. W. Leonard, St. Catherines, Ont.
F. D. L. Smith, Toronto, Ont.
That is the statement I have to make with respect to this matter. I think I have covered the field very well except to say this: I stated the other day that the association had half a million acres of land listed at the present moment, and that land is all listed within reasonable distance of the existing railways largely our own national railways. They are making some progress. The latest reports I have from them-and these reports are to be furnished monthly [DOT]-denote that they have 200 intending settlers ready to bring to western Canada to examine the lands that have been listed. They have agents in the United States, a very large number of agents, and undoubtedly these men will be under the control of the manager, Mr. Everett. If there is an element of danger to this government in trying to utilize and use the services of an organization of this kind-as my hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) pointed out-backed by the people I have mentioned so far as I know-because I have had no contradiction of this telegram of Sir John Willison's of the 30th September that there was full knowledge of the scheme that is now before the House-I have had no communication or no objection with the single exception of the one gentleman I have mentioned, Colonel John S. Denms. I still believe that a great many people in Canada think this is the proper method to handle privately owned land, along the existing lines of railway, which it is so desirable to bring under cultivation and have settled.
My hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) has suggested that we are not co-operating with the provincial governments. I think I told my hon. friend the other day that not only was I trying to co-operate with them, but that I visited them last summer and placed before them the very serious situation, in my opinion, that existed in Canada for the lack of an adequate population. I went to the province from which my hon. friend himself comes-I went as far west as British Columbia. I met the government in the Vancouver Hotel and discussed this matter with them. They are vitally interested, they are willing to co-operate; but they feel, perhaps, that it is a duty of the federal government to assume, in a large way, the financial responsibility of this work. With respect to the prairie provinces I did the same thing. Not only that but I called a conference last fall and asked representatives from every province in Canada to come here and discuss this very vital question in all its aspects; and these governments, so far as I know-I have had no intimation to the contrary-have endorsed this scheme outlined by my hon. friend. My hon. friend
Supply-Immigration

asked me why I recommend a scheme of this kind to the government? I felt, Mr. Chairman, that I had the backing, and that this government would have the backing, of the provincial governments; that we would also have the backing of these organizations that I have mentioned in a scheme of this kind when it had been so fully and clearly explained to them-as I was ready to believe had been done by this association and by so responsible a gentleman as Sir John Willison; because I think we can say with full assurance that Sir John Willison would make a fair presentation of the facts in a case of this kind. I felt too, and I think my hon. friends from western Canada will agree with me, that when a scheme of the kind was presented to westerners, who knew every phase of an enterprise of this character, they would be critical and examine the situation very carefully before lending support-such support as I have mentioned by way of resolutions passed by certain bodies-to an undertaking of this nature. Therefore, if I have made a mistake, if I have gone astray in making this recommendation, all I have to say is that I am in mighty good company.
Did the Alberta government fully endorse the proposition?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I know that the Alberta government was visited by these gentlemen and I know that previously they endorsed this scheme. I cannot say that 1 have in my possession letters from the Alberta government, since September 30, endorsing it.

Will the minister permit me one more question and I will not bother him any more. Has he official endorsation of this scheme, as set forth in their propaganda, from the Imperial government, the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Canadian National Railways, the provincial governments of Canada, and the banking institutions to which he has referred? If he has will he lay those endorsations on the table?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not endorsations from those organizations in writing. I have an endorsation from Colonel Amery, who was in charge of the Empire Settlement scheme, after Mr. M. A. Brown and Mr. Smith had laid this matter before him. However, let me in fairness, say this: Colonel Amery pointed out quite properly that before they would be prepared to lend full support to the scheme it would have to be endorsed by the government of Canada. Have I made myself clear?

Not at all. My hon. friend has made himself clear to this extent-he will correct me if I am wrong-that he has no official endorsation at all from any of these institutions to which he has referred and' to which the association's advertisement applies.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I followed
very closely the press despatches at the time this visit was made to western Canada. I saw no statement in the western newspapers that what was contained in the telegram from Sir John Willison was not true. I have no direct communications from the boards of trade or these various institutions I have mentioned.

My hon. friend does not catch my question. I asked him if he had the endorsation, as referred to in this propaganda, of the Imperial government, the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian government

never mind the telegram at all or the board of trade-these important official bodies upon which my hon. friend places so much importance and which he introduces in justification of his scheme.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

The Imperial government will assume a legal share of the cost of the welfare work.

And so on; inferring in this propaganda that the Imperial government, as my hon. friend's suggestion would infer, the Canadian Pacific and the other organizations, would assume part of the financial responsibility. Now apparently there is no such responsibility assumed by these bodies at all.

I am not sure whether the report brought back by Mr. Brown was confirmed by letter or not. However, one should speak carefully about matters of this kind. All I am sure is that we have a letter of the character I have mentioned from Colonel Amery, then head of the Overseas Settlement Board, saying that the scheme appealed to them, but of course it would require to have the endorsation of the federal government. With that, I will leave it. I will be very glad to examine my correspondence, to see just exactly what was said about that matter. Of course I am not responsible in every particular for all that may have appeared in that advertisement, nor do I wish to be held responsible. In the main, I think, perhaps, it is correct. I have tried to make myself clear with respect to the railways and with respect to the other individuals who were backing a scheme of this character.
I believe that my hon. friend asked the amount of money subscribed and paid up. I think practically one million and a quarter were subscribed, and so far, $150,000 of that amount has been paid up and used by this corporation, and that they will continue to subscribe, and that they are continuing to receive subscriptions, I am assured.

speechtext:
One hundred and fifty thousand dollars is the amount mentioned in the report I got from this association. So far as I am concerned, I will try to throw around the attempt, at all events, to settle the land and settle it successfully, carefully and economically, all the safeguards that are humanly possible to be placed around it. For years the organization known as the Salvation Army have been given a grant as my hon. friend well knows, of $25,000. No investigation has been held into the affairs of the army. I was one of the members of this House who voted that sum of money last year, but I would be unable to say just how that money is used. I believe it is used well. I believe they can
make good use of that $25,000. They do a splendid work, and I am again recommending that $25,000 be given to them. I have heard repeatedly commendation of the giving of this sum of money to this organization to engage in immigration work. So that the giving of a grant to the organization is not a new thing for the government which preceded us, nor for this government. This is in a somewhat larger way, and I say that I have not heard criticism of the grant to that organization. True they are religious. They are engaged to some extent in the land settlement scheme.

They are not getting a
ten per cent commission.
