No, not all.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: And full assurance is given that this money will not be taken in the way of profit. Let me say that if an arrangement is made with the association, an accounting of the disposition of funds will be made monthly. My hon. friend will say that is no particular protection, but I wish to impress upon the committee that every means of protection humanly possible will be adopted to prevent people being mulcted of their funds, or cheated in their settlement, and I hope that nothing of that kind will happen. My hon. friend will say that that is a pious hope and will not materialize.
Hear, hear.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
So far as I can see, I think this scheme has many advantages. It will help to settle a very difficult problem, because without it I fear we will have the same disjointed policy with respect to settling these lands and the same disappointment that we have had in the past. I have endeavoured to enlist every organization in immigration that was possible for me to enlist, hoping by the co-operation of all the people who are interested in this problem in Canada to work out a scheme of co-operation and co-ordination the effect of which would be advantageous to the people and government of that country. I stated the other day that any wide scheme of settlement involving hugii expenditures of money would not be warranted at this time, and I am of the same opinion today. In the light of the discussion we have had, I sometimes wonder whether it would not have been well to have gone very slow. It would have been a great disappointment to certain people in Canada had we done so.
Supply-Immigration

We have . gone moderately with this thing; we have endeavoured to evolve a scheme that will embrace every phase of settlement, bringing in people where they are required in urban centres, where a demand appears to exist for them and endeavouring to prevent unemployment during the long winter months, because we have to face in Canada the problem of seasonal employment with those six months of winter. I have sought to avoid the pitfalls of the past, first, by careful selection, second, by careful placing, in order to give those whom we bring into this country an opportunity to succeed.
As regards emigration, so far as we are able to get substantial returns, these would indicate that it is not so much the people who come to this country who are leaving it- and people are not leaving the country in such large numbers from western Canada as from eastern Canada-but rather our own sons and daughters, born and reared in Canada, who are going to the United States. Therefore, it behooves us that we be more careful than ever; that we exercise due care in selecting those whom we bring amongst us, because I do not see that we can entirely stop that flow to the United States, much as we would do so.
In conclusion, so far as possible in carrying out this scheme of immigration, every aspect of it, I will endeavour to exercise due care, first, in selection and, second, in placing, in order that we may have a well-balanced colonization scheme for the whole of Canada, including the area in northern Ontario about which my hon. friend has complained. We stand ready at any moment to co-operate with any provincial government on any scheme that will appeal to the federal authorities for the settlement of any area in any province, more particularly along the area served by the Grand Trunk Pacific railway through the older provinces of Quebec and Ontario. We welcome co-operation, and we will co-operate and work hand in hand in any scheme. In saying this, I am speaking largely on behalf of myself, but that would be my recommendation to the government.
I think I have covered all the phases in connection with this matter as regards the Canada Colonization Association. I shall be glad to have further light on immigration matters, and if possible so to adjust them as to meet with the approval of all hon. members.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I had not intended to take any part in this debate; but the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) brought my name into the discus-

sion, and he rather intimated that the Acting Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart) had taken upon himself to settle the entire question of the government's relation to the Canada Colonization Association, and that the matter had not	carefully considered by
the government as a whole. I just want to assure the House that co-operation in this matter was not lightly undertaken by the government but that it did receive the most careful consideration in Cabinet Council, before the minister finally decided to give the approval which he gave as to a limited measure of governmental assistance towards this Canada Colonization scheme.
I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to the responsibility which the government had in this matter. A government has to accept responsibility, not only for what it does, but for what it refuses or fails to do. In the matter of immigration, as members of the House well know, there is nothing that, perhaps, counts for so much as an effective organization, an organization that will bring together large bodies of influence that may have means and methods which even a government itself could not possibly have of helping to bring about the result desired. When we came into office, we found that our predecessors had done little or nothing with respect to immigration, in the months immediately preceding their going out of office. As a matter of fact, the whole immigration work of the government had been practically stopped. There was a demand, very naturally and properly, from all parts of Canada, that efforts should be made to stimulate immigration; that advantage should be taken of every possible agency towards that end. We found an organization which was already in existence, an organization, let me say at once, not composed of friends of the government. I think almost every name identified with it was that of a gentleman who had not been associated, so far as I am aware, with the administration; but the names were for the most part those of men who rank high in public confidence in this country. We found that organization in existence, and it was represented to us that it had been able to bring together certain of the large financial interests, the large transportation companies, and to a considerable extent the entire press of the country, as a combined agency to help to further it in its purpose, which was asserted to be the patriotic one of assisting, in getting settlers for the vacant lands of this country.
I ask hon. members: With an association of that kind in existence, representing to the

Supply-Immigration
government that our co-operation was required in order that they might get assistance from Great Britain under the British Empire settlement scheme, what position would the government have been in had it refused to countenance, in the slight degree in which we have countenanced it, this organization, and refused to agree to assist it in its welfare work?
I venture to say that hon. gentlemen who are condemning us to-day for some of the features of this organization which do not appeal to them, would have been the first and loudest in their denunciation of the government, had we at that time said: "We will not have anything to' do with this particular organization." And what would have been said? The reason would have been very speedily alleged or the motive asserted that the government had declined its co-operation because the gentlemen who for the most part composed the company, were not of the same political persuasibn as members of the administration.
I confess that when the whole plan was put before the government, I felt it was a serious matter for the government to lend assistance to an association as vast as this. On the other hand, considering the responsibility of refusing, and what a refusal might involve, namely, a possible complete crippling of the organization, and the destroying of the possibility of its securing assistance from the British government in connection with its work, I felt, on examining the personnel and above all having regard for the then president of the association, that the government was justified in lending the countenance it did to the association. I had interviews with Sir John Willison. The minister and myself met Sir John Willison and other members of the board at Toronto, and they outlined their plans very fully to us. The matter was thoroughly discussed in Council, and such assistance as we were giving, was given on the same basis as the British Empire Association was to give its assistance, and on a parity with what the organisation itself was also to give for its welfare work.
Let me again read this communication, because in a way it sums up the endorsation which the government felt it had from the different parties concerned. The minister has read it, but I shall refer to it again. The telegram was sent to me by Sir John Willison from Winnipeg after conversations we had had together on the subject, and after I had intimated in the clearest possible way to Sir John Willison that unless the government had the assurance that this scheme was
one which appealed to the western governments, and that it was a plan which was likely to meet with the general approval of parliament, irrespective altogether of the groups of which it was composed, we could not undertake to lend our co-operation to what it was proposing to do. On September 30th Sir John Willison sent me this telegram:
Have just completed tour of West. Have had conferences with four western governments and with grain growers and held many public meetings. Interviews with all governments most satisfactory and all meetings warmly sympathetic.
Now, I submit that no one who knows Sir John Willison and is aware of his standing, not only in this country, but throughout the British Empire, would suggest that a statement of that kind from him to the government of Canada was not equivalent to an endorsation of this plan on the part of the western governments and the people of the West generally. The telegram continues:
At Winnipeg meeting five hundred representative citizens called by James Stewart adopted with enthusiasm resolution offering plan Canada Colonization Association. Everywhere we emphasized action government in uniting all forces for immigration and settlement.
That was the strong point urged upon us by this association. It was pointed out by Sir John Willison and his associates that they had succeeded in bringing together into one organization agencies which were prepared to co-operate and which were so essential to bring immigrants to Canada, namely, the transportation agencies, the financial backing that was necessary, and the press of the country-three powerful and mighty influences, all ready to work together for the settlement of the unsettled areas. That was the note which Sir John Willison sounded, not only in conversation with the government, but publicly wherever he spoke on the subject.
Beatty has appointed Col. Dennis to represent Canadian Pacific on operating committee association,-
My hon. friend asks whether we have the endorsation of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I ask, in reply, what better form of endorsation could be given by this corporation than that which is implied in this statement, that its president had appointed Colonel Dennis to represent the Canadian Pacific Railway on the operating committee of the association. Then my hon. friend asks, have we any endorsation from any other source. What is the next statement in the telegram:
-and Chipman of Grain Growers Guide with approval Crtrar has agreed represent western farmers.
These are all names that are held in respect in this House and that carry weight with the government and with the country. I submit



Supply-Immigration
that with the class of representations that are contained in that telegram which were made to the government in regard to this association, had we refused to have anything to do With the organization, or to assist it to the small extent that we are-because in view of the fact that the organization has a subscribed capital of over a million dollars, $100,000 is relatively small when it covers everything for which we are obligated and which we have con" ditionally promised-our responsibility, in refusing to have anything to do with the organization would have been infinitely greater than the obligation which we have assumed in endeavouring to give the organization a start on its way,, and to help it successfully carry out the large purposes for which it is intended.

Mr. MACKENZIE. KING: When the committee rose at six o'clock I had been speaking of the responsibility of the government in the matter of lending the assistance which it promised to the Western Canada Colonization Association, and the still greater responsibility we would have assumed had we refused to have anything to do with that organization. 1 hope I made it plain that in promising a limited measure of assistance for the welfare work of the Association, the government was influenced by the importance of the work, the personnel of the association, and the large and

responsible interests represented by those gentlemen in this country.
I would like to say quite frankly that among the names that helped to inspire confidence so far as I personally was concerned was that of Sir John Willison, as president of the organization. I felt that Sir John Willison would not have associated himself as president with the Western Canada Colonization Association if its purpose was, as has been suggested in this debate that of some realty scheme, a land profits scheme of some kind or another, an agency other than of a patriotic and public-spirited character. Believing that the purpose of the organization was of a patriotic and public-spirited character, the government felt that it would justly incur a measure of disapproval, if it failed to encourage to the extent it did, an undertaking as vast as this, and which gave promise of such profitable results, possibly not all in a day, but in the course of time, by way of settling people on large tracts of land in this country.
When Sir John Willison retired from the presidency of the company, I confess that the members of the government felt a moment of concern with respect to the assistance that should be continued towards the organization, and we hesitated somewhat in oUr further relations with it. I remember particularly in the interviews I had with one or two members of the organization mentioning that we had gone into this matter to the extent we had, from purely public reasons, that if we had been governed by party considerations in any way, we would probably, as I indicated before recess, have had nothing whatever to do with the organization, as most of its personnel were gentlemen who were known to be opposed to the government. I stated that we had sought to take what we believed to be a broad patriotic stand and on this basis had recognized the association which our predecessors in office had been prepared to have dealings with. I pointed out that with the change that had come about as a consequence of Sir John Willison's resignation, it would be necessary for the company to give the government some further assurance of the confidence which it held in the minds of the people of the country. I spoke particularly of the complexion of the House of Commons and of the necessity in any great undertaking of this kind, of the government having the co-operation of the groups which were opposed to it. I pointed out that we had no desire whatever to deal with the immigration question on party lines; that we wished to have a policy broader than that of party and that we hoped and believed

Supply-Immigration
we could count upon the co-operation of hon. members in this House, in an endeavour to deal with this all important question, probably the most important we have, in a statesmanlike way. I received the assurance of the officers of the company that they had been in conference with the leaders of the groups opposite, and that the leaders were of the opinion that the government should give their support to the organization notwithstanding the change which had taken place in the presidency. I said that I would like to have some substantial evidence of that, and in the course of a short time I was presented with one or two letters which I shall read to the House, and I shall ask hon. members to consider from a reading of them whether the government was not right in believing that it was justified in continuing the co-operation which it had promised.
The first is a letter from the Right hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen), dated at Ottawa, Ontario, as recently as February 5, 1923. It is addressed to Mr. M. A. Brown, Vice-President of the Western Canada Colonization Association, Ottawa, Ontario. It was given to me by Mr. Brown with the statement that he had the permission of the right hon. leader of the Opposition to give this letter to the government. It reads as follows: Dear Mr. Brown,
Western Canada Colonization Association
You have asked me to give you my view as to the above Association.
When your organization was under way, the Honourable Mr. J. A. Calder, who was at that time Minister of Immigration and Colonization, looked with favour upon the establishment of a voluntary non-profit sharing company designed to serve as a colonizing agency of western farm lands, and as such to help to place and take care of immigrants who were to be intending settlers upon such lands.
Mr. Calder's attitude in this regard, which I believe was put in the form of a letter to the Association, was in harmony with the attitude of the government of the time.
I regarded such an Association as having a useful purpose to serve and could see then as I see now, no reason why it should not succeed.
Yours very truly,
Arthur Meighen.
At the same time I was handed by Mr. Brown a letter from my hon. friend the member for Brandon (Mr. Forke), and I may say that I had the same assurance from Mr. Brown at the time this letter was received by me, that it had been written with the expectation that the government would not hesitate to use it, if circumstances seemed to warrant its introduction into any of the debates. It reads as follows:
Ottawa, February 3, 1923.
Dear Mr. Brown,
Having taken into consideration the policy of the Canada Colonization Association, which is planned to
85i
effect the settlement of the vacant lands of the railway lines in Canada, I have no hesitation in endorsing the scheme so well suited to the requirements of the country. The need of new immigrants to settle our vacant lands is great and would tend to solve some of the problems that are now before us.
I am therefore of opinion that the government should do all in its power to assist the Association in this important enterprise.
Yours very sincerely,
Robert Forke.
That communication is in entire accord with the speech which the hon. leader of the Pro-, gressive group made in this House a night or two ago.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that these two communications are to all intents and purposes an endorsation of the Western Canada Colonization Association, an endorsation given in the same spirit and with the same knowledge of the organization, as the government had. I think hon. gentlemen opposite who have given these communications to the Western Canada Colonization Association have done so with precisely the same motive as the government had, in giving such endorsation as it gave, in promising co-operation with the British Empire Settlement Association in its immigration scheme. May I say that I think that had all hon. members of this House the knowledge of this association, and the purpose of its work, and the information concerning what it has accomplished in bringing together the different elements whose co-operation are so essential to success in immigration, their view of its possible service would have been precisely what the view of the government has been and the view expressed also in the two communications from the respective leaders of the groups opposite., which I have read to the House.
If, as a matter of fact, it should now appear that in any particular the Western Canada Colonization Association is not fulfilling the spirit as well as the intent of the letter of the representations and the undertakings they gave to the government, that would be a good and sufficient reason for the government to consider at this time whether further assistance should be given to the organization. I submit further, that such changes as have taken plat 5 since would be a reason for the government coving with increased caution in the matter if any assistance it might give the association; that having taken the precautions that the government has taken to ascertain from the leaders of the groups opposite how far they also had confidence in this organization, and having before it the communications which I have just read, the government has, in this
[Mr. Forke. 1
matter, acted in a manner which is best serving the interests of the country. But if it should now appear that this organization has in any way departed from its original purpose, if in any way it is departing from the representations which it made to the government- and on the basis of which such co-operation as we have given was given-then there would be good and sufficient reason why we should consider whether that co-operation should be extended any further. I confess, having regard to all of the circumstances, to the fact that the immigration problem is par excellence the great problem concerning this country at the present time, having regard to the fact that this association has brought together the different interests that should work in a coordinated fashion in the matter of immigration, that there would be a very great responsibility in the government declining at this stage to have anything further to do with the organization. But if hon. members have not confidence in it, if there is any reason to mistrust the organization at this particular stage, then I would say quite frankly that the government is prepared to consider just how much further, if at all, it should extend the co-operation which it has already promised in good faith, and in what it believes to be the best interests of the country.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That association was organized as a non-profit sharing, voluntary organization. As such it was looked on with favour; but assistance, by the government, and any system of inter-locking responsibility of the government with it was refused. Presented in the character it was then, for the purposes it then had, by itself and without any responsibility on the govern-' ment's part and without any assistance from the government, it was favoured. In that sense I favoured it then; I have not changed my position in regard to the matter at all. But to say that because one does look with favour on the activities of a voluntary company, resting on its own feet, not asking to be supported by the state, not asking that
the state share the responsibility of its work -favouring a company on that basis is one thing, the government policy is something. else altogether. There is no word in my letter binding me, or intimating in the least degree that I favoured assistance by the government of Canada or that I favoured the gpvernment of Canada entering into some arrangement with this organization whereby government officers would assume a share of the responsibility for the work of the organization in the selling of lands, or in the purchase of lands by immigrants-nothing in the world in my letter favoured any such policy. I am quite prepared, I say, to stand by what I said then, because it is no doubt what we said when we were in power. But what we did when we were in power is wholly different from this proposal; and what I said at that time is wholly different from what is said by the Prime Minister.
Now, I have not had the advantage of hearing anything else from the Prime Minister himself, but in the course of the debate I have heard it said that nothing was done by the late administration in the way of immigration, and that there were great calls for immigration activities in the time of the late administration. Well, there were calls for many things during the time of the late administration. It was a time of calls all over the Dominion, but the only thing that was not called for was immigration. I do not remember ever hearing the call from anybody for special activities in immigration at that time. Here, as in every country in the world, the volume of unemployment was great-great in almost all classes of employment-and there was considerable suffering as a result. It is true we had the least unemployment relatively of any country in the world. It is true we had less unemployment even than the great republic to the south of us though one would expect that in the reaction and the relapse from the war we would suffer more than the great republic.. Up to the end of 1921 our share of unemployment was less than theirs, but that is not the case to-day. Our share of unemployment now is much more than theirs relatively to population. Still we had large numbers out of work and there was no pressure for great immigration effort.
Immigration at that time though was not dead. Immigration at that time was all it could be expected to be so soon after the war. We had some 117,000 people come to this country in the year that succeeded the war; that is to say in the first fiscal year after the war. We had some 140,000 people in the succeeding year, and last year, part of it

I do not know whether 1 can make myself plain in any fewer words than the right hon. leader of the Opposition has taken to state his position. I have no apologies for anything I have done. I have not changed my mind in any particular. I wrote that letter in perfect good faith and I think I could write it with a clear conscience to-day. I had no idea at that time as to what the government was going to do, and understood nothing of the relations which existed between the government and the Western Canada Colonization Association. I do not 
know whether I drew my letter just as closely as the right hon. leader of the Opposition did, but I am certain the intention I had was the same as his intention. We had no difference in our idea, which was to convey to the people at large that we thought there was merit in the scheme. I think so yet. I may be wrong. I think I said when speaking in the beginning of the debate, that if the scheme could not stand criticism and investigation by all means condemn it, but what I had to find fault with, and do find fault with to-day, i3 that the scheme had been condemned without trial or investigation in any quarter. We know something about the scheme and understand something about its workings, and, as with every other scheme, unless the personnel of the men who are connected with it and who are carrying out its working is what it ought to be, then perhaps the scheme will fall down. I am quite prepared to stand on what I said in that letter. It had nothing to do with the arrangement proposed by the government at the present time. That will have to stand on its own merits, and in that con-nectioh it might be thought that there was something mysterious about the question I was asking the Premier about another letter. I know that Mr. Brown had two or three hundred letters from most of the prominent people in this country. It is part of the stock in trade in launching any scheme to get the endorsation of men whose opinions are worth having, and I thought perhaps the Premier would read another letter which I had in mind.

The debate has
centred recently around the question of the ^Western Canada Colonization Association. I do not desire to say very much with regard to that company, as I think there has been a great deal of criticism offered. I must protest against the government subsidizing any private company of this character. It seems to me that, with the Soldier Settlement Board in existence, with the government agents throughout this country and the United States

and Europe, we ought to have sufficient machinery to do the work that is required to be done along these lines, and we ought not to commit ourselves to any private company that undoubtedly has, in one form or another, profit and gain in view. The Acting Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart) referred to the fact that the Salvation Army is receiving funds for which no accounting is required. It seems to me if this is so it is rather a thing in itself to be inquired into. We do not need to condemn any organization, the Salvation Army or any other, but we say there ought to be a strict accounting for every dollar that is spent by this parliament, and we ought to know exactly the purpose to which it is being applied.
In considering this matter we shall require to go a great deal more deeply into the question than simply dealing with one particular company. I cannot agree with the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) in his statement that the drying up of the stream of immigration must be laid at the door of the present government. I take it that there are larger economic and social forces at work, and that, whatever government was in power at the present time, we would have very similar results. Personally, I am not opposed to immigration as such. The member for Springfield	(Mr.	Hoey)	told	us	theother day of the very great resources we had in Winnipeg and the western country. I	think	we all	agree	on	that.Any man who has lived in the West is fully cognizant of the almost unparalleled resources that exist in that western country, and I think we all recognize that with those resources we have room for millions of people in the West. No one disputes that; but that is not the point that we are arguing at the present time. The question before us is whether we should adopt an active immigration policy in face of existing conditions at home. It seems to me that the first duty of this parliament is to safeguard the interests of those already in the country. It is not that some of us are opposed to immigration that we oppose such a policy as this; but we say:	"Why go on with this policy when
there are other alternatives that we might adopt?" We have been told that we ought to pump immigrants in. We, who question the policy are on the ground of common sense when we say that it is more essential to Btop the leaks than to keep pumping people in. It might be all very well to pump them in if we proceed at the same time to stop the leaks; but it would seem the part of good, sound common sense to stop the leaks first. It is not good policy to continue to expend
large sums of money while people are leaking out faster than we can pump them in.
We might clarify our thinking if we should ask who is really to benefit by this immigration policy. The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler)) took rather high moral grounds when he said that we have no exclusive claim to this country, and that we ought to admit people who, perhaps, are in inferior positions in other lands. I am quite willing to admit that that is true, although I notice that the hon. member for North Waterloo was rather inclined to think we white people had exclusive claims to this country. I do not know how he reconciles that	with the broader idea; but I
do not think we can contend that we alone have exclusive claim to the northern half of this American continent. It is, however, laid upon us who are here to see to it that large floods of immigrants are not permitted to destroy or to lower permanently the standard of living of the people in this country.
Although we protest that we are doing this for the sake of the immigrant, again and again in those self-same speeches, we come back to the point that we are doing this in order that we may get more people to carry our load. Let us be frank and say that we are asking for more immigrants in order that they may help us in this country and assist this country. I am not sure that that is not a very good reason, for the adoption of such a policy; but let us be frank and say that we are looking after ourselves in this regard. That raises a still further question whether all people or all classes of people in Canada are to be benfited by such immigration, or whether we are benefitting only certain classes. It seems rather peculiar that the great masses of the labour people of this country and of the farming people of the western part of Canada should be opposed to bringing in immigrants. Under these circumstances we should ask ourselves whether the incoming of immigrants at the present time would not tend to benefit simply a few. Undoubtedly the transportation systems would benefit .very largely, and I fancy from the telegram which was read twice to-day and which was emphasized, that the transportation interests and the financial interests have been exercising a very strong pressure upon the Acting Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart) and upon the government in this regard. It is two or three years ago since Lord Shaughnessy first told us that we ought again to adopt a progressive immigration policy, and about two years ago now, Mr. Beatty, president of the Canadian Pacific, came out very definitely with this

The most urgent and essential need to-day is increase in population, not only to provide traffic for the railways, but also to help pay our enormous national indebtedness.
He said further:
In reference to the 300,000 Ukrainians in western Canada, in which it is stated that these people of sturdy farming stock from central Europe have four large educational institutes.
And so on. He claims that these are the people whom we ought to bring in-the sturdy peasants from Central Europe. Still further, not satisfied with this, Mr. Beatty urges:
. What progress can Canadian industry make if the skilled mechanic is to be practically shut out? And Without Canadian industry where are we to find exports for the Canadian Merchant Marine?
I would like to ask: What attitude are these transportation interests themselves taking in this matter of retaining the people in this country and building up our Canadian industry? I have received a communication from a union of mechanics from my own city of Winnipeg, which states:
The Manitoba Free Press of Friday the second of February carried a despatch stating that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company had let contracts in the States for the construction of sixteen locomotives, and that in the meantime their own plants were working to capacity, whilst as a matter of fact at that very time the Angus shops were closed down, and its working staff on the streets.
This organization passed the following resolution which was forwarded to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the Acting Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock):
Whereas, continual attacks are being made upon the earnings of railway workers and,
Whereas, the shopmen employed by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have been on continuous short time for the past two years, and,
Whereas, the highest possible earnings of a skilled mechanic working every hour the shops were open during the last two years have averaged only $24.61 per week, and the highest possible earnings of a mechanic's helper have averaged only $16.90 per week, and,
Whereas, according to published statements the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have during the last crop movement had the largest earnings in the history of the road, and notwithstanding, have kept the mechanical staff on short time and periodically closed the shops,
Now, therefore, be it resolved that this mass meeting of Canadian Pacific shopmen strongly protest this action of the company, and demand that the transportation industry of the country be organized upon a basis that will ensure a decent standard of living for the permanent staff engaged in it.
If we turn from the West to the East, T have also from the International Association of Machinists in Montreal, a resolution along somewhat similar lines:
[Mr. Woodsworth.l
We understand that contracts for some forty-eight lake freighters have recently been contracted for, by companies operating on our lakes and rivers, with firms outside the country and it would appear to us that such business methods are not in the best interests of the citizens of this country. The shipyard workers of this country have demonstrated their ability to build good ships and the boats they produced are, in their particular class, amongst the finest, in point of workmanship, to be found oh the waters of the globe. Thousands of these workmen have been thrown out of employment, or have been forced to accept temporary work in other lines, through the closing down of our shipyards and this condition obtains, to a great extent, because of the failure on the part of shipping companies, operating in Canada, to patronize Canadian shipyards. It is also a fact that many of our best shipyard mechanics have left the country in search of employment in that line and, undoubtedly, many others will be compelled to do likewise, unless some action is taken to prevent it.

January 30, 1923. That was sent to me with a request that the matter be brought before parliament at the first opportunity. Now, when we have men in the employ of these transportation com-*panies, both in the East and in the West, bringing in resolutions along this line, outlining facts that show a condition of affairs in which large numbers of our own Canadian citizens find it impossible to obtain a decent living in this country, it seems to me that there is something to be attended to before there is adopted any policy looking to the bringing in of more people. In my constituency of Centre Winnipeg, I think there have been thousands of people during the past year who have been forced to go south of the line in order to get work. Among these people there were the very best mechanics to be found in this country, and to such an extent has this emigration taken place that we are now told there may be a shortage. There is not yet, however, any shortage in Canada in this direction.
I might refer to the different classes of immigrants that we have had brought into Canada in the past. Roughly speaking, during the fifteen years in which our immigration was at full tide, one-third of the immigrants came from the United States, one-third from Great Britain, and one-third from the various countries of Europe. Undoubtedly those who have come to us from the western states have been amongst our very best citizens, from the standpoint of the farming industry. A very considerable number of them sold out their holdings in the United States at high prices and invested in our Canadian lands, which they were able to purchase comparatively cheap. A good many of them brought considerable equipment with them, and from

Supply-Immigration
the material point of view at least their incoming meant a great deal, especially to the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. Those, however, who know these provinces and have experience of them in more recent-years, know that very many of these American citizens are already travelling back over the boundary. Some of them are selling out their lands in this country because they want to get back to the homeland south of the line. A good many, of course, are remaining. But it would seem as though tliere are a sufficient number of people in the leading western states who now know of the opportunities offered by western Canada that, if our taxation could be brought down and implements could be put within reach of the farmers at reasonable prices, there would not be the slightest doubt that we should gain steadily a stream of immigration from the western states.
The second group of people to whom I referred came from Great Britain. These were of two classes: first of all, those who came from the rural districts. And we have never had a very large immigration from rural England; a larger number have come from rural Scotland. But I would suggest that those who come from rural England, if we can get any, are not going to solve our problems in western Canada; for I would remind my Progressive friends here that a good many of these people are accustomed to standards of living much superior to those which a large percentage of our farmers can afford to give them in this country. I would remind my hon. friends that these people, too, are accustomed to membership in unions of agricultural labourers, that they have worked much shorter hours than they would be required to work in this country, and have been used to very much better accommodation than can be found on a great many of our western farms. And I know that a good many of my farmer friends in the West feel that agricultural workers from England are rather a difficult class to handle to-day under present conditions.
What about their Scotch whiskey?

Well, in the dry territories that may be a very serious matter, too. There is another thing which I think a good many of our farmers are realizing more and more clearly. In the older days when immigration was flowing freely to this country and when there was a steady movement from eastern Canada to the West, it was comparatively easy for the western farmer to secure
hired men for a short period. Young fellows without the encumbrances of a family were eager to get a start in the new land and were willing to be hired for a few months at a time; then if they so desired they could take up homesteads for themselves. To-day the farmers on the prairies are having to compete more and more with the manufacturers in the city for hired labour; and the labour men in the cities are accustomed to shorter hours than those customary on the farm. A good many of them have families and expect that provision shall be made for themselves and their families where they are expected to reside. In this way, we shall have to recognize that the problem of agricultural labour in western Canada is bound to be a very serious one in the days to come. We cannot depend upon a steady supply of transient labour which we can use for a few months and then get rid of. In the older countries farming has become fully self-supporting; it should be in no sense parasitic.
Now, although in my judgment at least the manufacturers and the trans-
9 p.m. portation companies of this country have exploited the farmer, at the same time I think that in a great many ways our farmers have existed at all only by exploiting their hired help and their own wives and children. If I understand the temper of these western farmers, they are beginning to take the stand that they are not going indefinitely to exploit their wives and children. A great many of the farm labourers, too, are beginning to realize that they have a right to expect that if they are going to work on farms they must have the assurance that they shall work for twelve months in the year and, as my hon. friend (Mr. Hoey) implied, that some arrangement must be made to provide them with permanent homes. In some way we shall have to overcome the difficulty in connection with seasonal labour.
Anyone who has come into close contact with the immigration from the Old Land recognizes that a large proportion of our English immigration has come to us from the cities. It is quite true that a certain number of these immigrants declared that they were going to work on the farms; but again and again they have drifted back into the cities. The mere fact that they declare their destination to be the farm does not in any way bind them to stay there. Some of us who have lived in the cities for years, and who have had to do with the welfare work in those centres of our population, know perfectly well that a large proportion of the people with whom we have to deal are Old Country im-
Will the hon. member explain how they were "driven" from the lands?

I shall be very glad to do so. They were brought here on the express understanding that they should be allowed certain privileges, should be given the right to practise their own religious beliefs and to live in communities. It was against their religion to take the oath of allegiance; they were what might be called Eastern Quakers. For a time they lived in Saskatchewan, building up considerable communities there. Then there came into office another Minister of the Interior who insisted that they should register, each man for his own property, and should take the oath of allegiance. This was opposed to their ideals and to the understanding that they had with the government when they come to this country. The great majority of them, rather than give up their religious beliefs and their peculiar ideals, gave up their lands, valued, I think, at some $10,000,000, and, for the most part, went further west and purchased lands at the junction of the Columbia and Kootenay rivers. In this connection I want to suggest to the committee that certain problems were introduced into the country by the emigration of these peculiar peoples from other lands. We still have the Doukhobors in British Columbia, and w7e still have their peculiar religious and moral ideas to deal with. By importing large numbers of these sectaries and

[DOT]others we may increase our exports for the time being, but sooner or later we shall have to face the problem of absorbing them into our Canadian citizenship.
Take another group, also a peculiar people, the Mennonites. Of Holland or German extraction, these people had lived for a good many years in Russia. About forty years ago they came to this country and settled in southern Manitoba. They were among our very best settlers. From Manitoba they colonized certain sections of Saskatchewan. Then there came the question of the public schools, which became acute at the time of the war; and the action of the Manitoba and Saskatchewan governments on that question has driven thousands of these people away down into Mexico where they are seeking freedom in the exercise of their religious beliefs. Very recently the business men of Winnipeg, realizing the financial loss involved, got together in an effort to induce the government to change its policy so that these Mennonite colonies might be retained in Manitoba. I am not sure that we can gain a great deal by allowing tens of thousands of Mennonites who have been here for forty years to go to another country and then bring in fresh streams of Poles from another country. It may be quite true that Mennonites are a brand of Protestant while Poles are a brand of Roman Catholic. In other words, we have a change of religious belief, but we have the same European peasant to deal with; aiid that is a difficulty that we face throughout western Canada.
Take the Ukrainians, the largest group we have. I am not one who thinks that the Ukrainian people are undesirable settlers. There are some 300,000 of them in the West, and they have on the whole made good, especially when they were settled on anything like decent land. There are some of them in Manitoba on poor lands, but on the whole they came in with very little capital; they worked hard and now most of them have their lands with very little debt. They had low standards of living, but. they persisted and a great many of them to-day own their own homes. During the war it began to dawn upon us in Canada, as it did in the United States, that this talk about all these people going into the melting pot was a lot of nonsense. As they said in the States, they may be put into the melting pot, but they refuse to melt; and unless we are careful in this country we shall have a Balkanized Canada. Down in eastern Canada you have had some trouble in the past, I understand, as between French-speaking and English-speaking people.
Mr. MARLER; When did we have any trouble between the English-speaking and the French-speaking people in the province of Quebec?

I speak largely from hearsay, but I live in the West and there has never been an election when I have not heard of considerable strain and stress between the English-speaking and the French-speaking people of eastern Canada.
Mr. MARLER; If the hon. member is referring to the province of Quebec, I absolutely deny any such charge. There is the best of feeling between the French and English in the province of Quebec.
I think the hon. member has misunderstood me. I am not speaking of the province of Quebec. I spoke of eastern Canada.
You said Quebec.
If I did, then I withdraw. I had not thought of the province of Quebec. I was thinking of eastern Canada when I spoke.
Is the hon. member referring to Nova Scotia? If he can point to any trouble that has occurred between the French and the English in the province of Nova Scotia, it is more than I can.
I am not speaking of the province of Nova Scotia.

I for one am glad to think that we have had a decided effort to promote something of a better feeling- and I think the effort has been very largely successful-between these two great races in Canada, so that we may sit here to-day in absolute friendship. But I would like to suggest that there are problems-religious, racial, and linguistic-that we must have in the West if we continue to import large numbers of people from all the countries of Europe. That is the point I wish to make, and we have to be careful on that particular score.
There is another matter to which reference should be made, and that is the relationship which exists between the people in the city and the people in the country. Here in eastern Canada-I hope I will not have to say whether it is in Ontario or Quebec-but generally speaking in eastern Canada, the farmers have stayed more largely on the farms than they have on the prairies. Out in the West there is a continual drifting backward and forward between the cities and the country. A very considerable number of people who have tried to homestead in western Canada have drifted back into our cities. I was in a little town in northern Manitoba a few years ago and discovered that no less than seventy Ukrainian farmers were living in that little town, bankrupt. They had gone out on a homestead, had tried to make a living, had failed, and had drifted back into this little town.
A few years ago in the city of Winnipeg we had a very careful investigation with regard to some hundreds of foreigners who were being more or less kept by the city. If my memory serves me, no less than ninety-four per cent of these foreigners had come to this country with the full intention of farming but had stayed for a little while in the city in order to get together a little ready cash. They had been induced to purchase homes in the city, to invest in real estate and that kind of thing, and had been diverted from their original purpose. Now it is all very well to suggest that it is comparatively easy for a man to start without capital on the western prairies. I know some of the pioneers have done that. I know some of them endured great hardships, and that some of them are to-day fairly well to do, and some people are inclined to say: What I did, others may do. But there are not nearly such good opportunities to-day in western Canada for starting to farm without capital as there were thirty or forty years ago. In the first place,at that time land could be got absolutely free or very cheap. I remember when 
you could buy land for three or four or five dollars an acre. That land to-day costs from $15 to $25 an acre. In the old days there was more or less of a local market, but today buying and selling has been so thoroughly organized into a great commercial machine that as soon as a man steps off his own farm he comes into the grip of that great machine, and it is not easy for him to make his own way independently. Further than that, in the old days it was comparatively easy for a man to work at something else until he could get a start on his farm. Many worked as section men and many worked as hired men for a few years. That work is becoming more and more difficult to get, and so it is not easy for a man to go out at the present time and make a start with a small capital. The Acting Minister of Immigration has suggested that the men with $1,500 or $2,000 might make a start. I may say that a committee that looked into this thing from a very practical standpoint in Winnipeg a few years ago came to the conclusion that a man could not make a start in this country on less than $5,000 or thereabouts, and maintain a decent standard of living, and keep clear of debt. A man must have his living for a year or two before his farm will begin to produce. We have heard some glowing words from the province of Manitoba. I have here a paper which came to my hand the other day. It is the votes and proceedings of the legislative assembly of Manitoba, and in a resolution on the order paper I notice this statement:
And whereas owing to financial conditions existing in this province, more than one hundred and fifty of our elementary schools are closed at the present time, and children deprived of elementary education-
It is quite true, as the hon. member for Springfield said, that we have a magnificent parliament building in the city of Winnipeg, but we have also one hundred and fifty schools in the province closed, for lack of financial support. This is a serious thing when you consider the welfare of the next generation of Canadians.
Here is an extract from a letter which came to me the other day from one of the best informed social workers in the city of Montreal. He says:
Why is it said to be so easy to find suitable foster homes for children imported from England, when every day of every year children already in Canada, many of them born Canadians, are being huddled like so many chickens into human chicken houses.
I have been studying the history of the English poor law very closely this term, and I have become quite convinced that for both economic and social reasons the Dominion government will sooner or later have to establish a statistical department to collect information as to the extent and the nature of public and private assistance being given throughout the

Supply-Immigration
Dominion. If it is not done we are going to wake up some day and find that a very considerable portion of our population is always dependent, and then we shall wonder how and why it all happened.
I have a resolution here from an organization of the workers, also in the city of Montreal, which reads:
Be it resolved that we condemn the policy of inducing people to immigrate to this country whilst thousands of our citizens are unable to secure employment and are receiving no assistance from the governments, and that we take steps to notify the workers of Great Britain and Europe of the conditions they will be faced with if they come to Canada at this time.
I may say that I also have similar resolutions from the West, and I would like to inform the Acting Minister of Immigration and Colonization that there is to-day an active propaganda being carried on in the newspapers in the Old Country by the working people of this country to offset the proposed immigration policy of Canada. Further than that, I may say that on the floor of the House of Commons in Great Britain the opposition, which as you all know is the Labour party, is definitely opposed to this policy of overseas settlements and in particular to the scheme of taking Old Country children and shipping them out to the dominions.
Now, what are the prospects of the future. A good deal has been said about this policy being fostered by the financial interests and by the transportation companies. As to that I should like to quote a few lines from a statement by Sir Edmund Walker in the Financial Post of February 9.
We both wish to discriminate as to the class of immigrants we permit to land on our shores, and we surely should do so but our salvation throughout all North America depends upon a reasonably free supply of unskilled labour.
We must produce cheaper and we must produce more.
Again:
We cannot pretend that we did not know that because of war debts we must for a generation or more work harder for longer hours, and with more intense application not only because of the vast debt but because we have lost the labour of those who fell in order that we should live.
And again:
We are lucky among the nations who created war debts in owing ours mostly to ourselves.
And perhaps it is quite in line with that last statement when Sir Edmund Walker states in the annual report of the Bank of Commerce :
A domestic debt merely means the transfer by a tax of so-called money from one citizen to another.
Which is, as I understand it, that we must allow immigrants to come in here to help us to pay our debts. But we pay them to ourselves-rone set of people, through the medium of money, pay to another set of people
here in Canada. We have been told again and again that prosperity is just round the corner. We have been told that ever since the war stopped, and yet there are very few gentlemen who have come forward to tell us how that prosperity is going to come about, or what the basis is on which they found their predictions. It is said that in order to secure prosperity we must have larger markets. But where are those markets? It is said that we must be willing to compete. I would like to suggest to the farmers here that they may find it extremely difficult to compete with the Argentine, and with Russia and Roumania when those countries have begun to produce again. In order to compete we must rid ourselves of the loads with which we are now burdened.
. The fact is that the time demands constructive measures, the time demands radical changes in our whole system, and the difficulty is that our government, and our governing classes, are, as the Americans say "standing pat," or they are trying to encourage us with the old slogans. Twenty years ago we were told that immigration was going to solve our problems, and it did to a very considerable extent help in opening up this country. But my question is: Are we going to be able to repeat what took place twenty years ago? The conditions are altogether different to-day. At that time we had a country largely undeveloped; at that time we were drawing our funds from Europe in order to build our railroads; at that time we were building every little village into a town, and every town into a city-there were all sorts of opportunities. To-day our railways are built; we have more mileage by many thousands of miles- than we need. To-day our factories are built and many of them are standing idle. To-day our cities are built up; we say that we have altogether too large an urban population. It was because of this incoming of large financial resources, as well as of the incoming of large numbers of people, that at that time we had a chance to make such rapid development. But the whole world situation is changed. At that time we had markets which are absolutely closed to us at the present day. At that time we had a comparatively light load to carry; to-day we are overburdened with debt. Again I should like to ask, if in the West our vei"1' best English speaking people-many of them Canadians with farm training,-are not able to make things go, how in the name of common sense can we expect untrained Britishers to come over here without capital and make things go where the Canadian born have to a large extent failed.

Some of us-and I think I may say that in this regard I represent a very considerable section of workers across the country

suggest that there are other alternatives than those proposed by the government. The Acting Minister of Immigration and Colonization says that we have to back up a colonization company in order to get rid of our unsold and unused lands. I would like to suggest that there is another policy altogether. The fact is that our land policy in this country has been largely a failure. Those who first outlined that policy had the hope that in Canada we would have large numbers of people, each man living on his own land. That was the idea of the homestead-each man would be a freeholder. What is the situation to-day? A very considerable percentage of the farms are mortgaged; our farmers are not freeholders. The dream of those who founded these regulations has not been realized and worse than that-to those who would today come into this country we cannot offer the free lands that were offered years ago. I would like to ask, Mr. Chairman, whether we should not say that these great areas of agricultural land should be for the people who are actually going to live on them and proceed to do one of two things-either expropriate them, or else tax them so heavily that they would be forced into use. It is because we have been looking at this thing from the standpoint of the investor rather than from the standpoint of the settler that we have not achieved the success we should have achieved. I remember going a few years ago-it must be ten years now-to the then Premier of one of the western provinces and talking with him over a scheme for bringing settlement a little bit closer, and placing certain social opportunities within the reach of the settlers in the various districts. "Yes," he said, "this is very desirable. It would mean that the children would all get an education. It would mean that the women would have opportunity of having a doctor when they were ill. It would mean they would have some neighbours near them, and it would mean a great, deal more production in the country." But he asked "How are you going to finance it?"
I suggested that a few cents more per acre added to the wild lands tax would finance the whole proposition. Throwing up his hands he said, "You could never do that, the American investors are already protesting against the wild lands tax."

Surely the hon. member is aware of the situation around Winnipeg, where no man will hold land to-day and pay taxes 
very long, if he can get rid of it. The hon. member knows that very well.

I know there are tens of thousands of acres being held to-day all over western Canada by men who are not using these lands, and if they were taxed heavily enough those people would be forced to get rid of them, and I would say that the duty of any government that is attempting to solve this problem-
The hon. member says that if those lands were taxed heavily enough, you would get rid of them.
Yes.
I would like to know who would be found to buy them.

On two occasions in the last few days the minister (Mr. Stewart) who has charge of this very important Department of Immigration, has laid his policy before the House, and I am sure that it has been listened to with a great deal of interest by members here assembled, and that throughout the country a considerable degree of attention has been paid to his announcement. I do not care to level any particular degree of criticism against the special point raised this afternoon so effectively by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). Perhaps enough regarding that particular aspect of the question has been said for the present. I may remark, however, in passing, that it seemed to require the united efforts of the minister and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to refute some of the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, and even then they did not cover them with any degree of finality; leaving entirely untouched the question raised by that hon. member regarding the tremendous amount in commissions which would be paid
Supply-Immigration

out by this government if they tied themselves up to this scheme, and the very large profits which would accrue to the Western Canada Colonization Association by means of the very liberal commissions which they would receive.
I wish to pass on to say a word or two regarding the general nature of the minister's policy. I do not find it pleasant work to criticise any hon. gentleman in a severe manner, and I do not fear that I shall transgress beyond the bounds of courtesy in dealing with this subject. But I must confess that I have been considerably disappointed by the announcement made, after a great deal of eager expectation on the part of the country, by the minister, who, I presume, has given very careful and studious consideration to one of the largest and most momentous problems which confronts this country at the present time. I do not think any person would, perhaps, be justly blamed for saying that "the mountain had laboured"-and hon. members know the rest of the proverb. However, much criticism may be levelled against the minister's policy, or lack of policy, from this quarter of the House, I do not expect any more severe strictures will be hurled at his head than those which have already come from members of the party sitting behind him. Very frank, very outspoken, and I might almost say, very bitter, were some of the criticisms advanced by the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill), who, in the frankest possible way, informed the minister that he was permitting the railways of this country to bleed the people white; that he was responsible to a large degree for the emigration of those Canadian citizens who have sought homes in the United States, from the fact that he and his government had not adhered to their pre-election pledges brought forward in such a forceful way through their election platform of 1919, and thus, after deceiving the people, had brought them to a state worse than their former condition had been. Then, following up that very acrimonious dissertation by the hon. member for Pontiac, came one couched m, perhaps, smoother language, but none the less with a barb concealed in it, or, perhaps, I should not say "concealed," for it really was very apparent, when the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) arose and also raked over the minister for several r*ins of omission and commission. So, per-liaps, I am not altogether wrong in saying that however much criticism may be advanced against the policy of the Immigration department from this end of the chamber, nothing more severe is likely to be said during 
this debate than that which has already emanated from his friends.
What I am, however, particularly exercised about as regards this policy, lies in a point touched upon by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth), who said that unfortunately-and I desire very heartily to concur in his adverb-during the last few years, immigration to this country from Europe has proceeded, not from the northern section of that continent, not from the British Isles, but from the southern and central portions of Europe. I do not consider that the present policy of the minister in this respect is altogether a wise one. If one sifts it right down, it amounts to this. He has permitted Australia and South Africa to skim off the cream from the British Isles of the immigration which we might expect to flow to this country, if proper efforts had been put forth in time to bring it here, and now lie has recourse, through his agents in central and eastern Europe, to endeavouring to bring immigrants here from Hungary and Poland.
There is another, broader and more important aspect by far, to my mind, from which this question of immigration should be viewed by the people of Canada. We are building for the future; we must consider what is going to happen to this country of ours if we allow a very large section in the middle of it to be filled up by immigration which has been brought into the prairies for the past number of years. We in British Columbia have previously informed this House of our grievance as regards oriental immigration. Our principal, our vital objections to that class of immigration are that by no manner of means can it be made to assimilate into our population and become in any true sense of the word Canadian. I greatly fear that there is in the prairie sections of this Dominion, a very large element which it will be found very difficult to absorb into our Canadian population and to imbue with any true national spirit. Seventy-five or eighty or, perhaps, more languages are spoken by these people, and the greatest mistake we have made, possibly-
