I think it is only fair to say that that inference might very readily have been drawn from what the minister told the House, but I am glad to hear the statement which he has made now. Even so, the fact remains that he informed the House that he was endeavouring to procure immigration from Hungary and Poland, and that so far he has not apparently become enamoured of the idea of exerting any great amount of energy or of expending what might be called a comparatively large sum of money in encouraging immigration from the British Isles.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I should like to put my hon. friend right. There are twelve agencies continually working in the British Isles. Moreover, we have been putting on a propaganda that up to date has been bringing results. Within the past few days a very considerable number have been landed from the British Isles. There is no continental movement at the moment, and I want to add that there is no restriction on the people coming from the British Isles, while we have a restriction on those from the Continent.

I should be very much surprised indeed if any minister in this House did inform this assembly that there were restrictions to be placed on the people from the British Isles while freer measures were to be accorded those from other countries. I am quite aware of the fact the minister states. What I did say, however, was that the minister frankly admitted this afternoon that Australia and South Africa had got into the British Isles before this country and had diverted to themselves a large stream of British immigration; and that up to the present very few results have apparently come from any system of encouragement which the minister has been giving to immigration from that source. I very cordially endorse what was said the other night by the member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) who spoke of the sources from which we should seek immigration. We should secure all the people whom we can get from Great Britain, France, Hungary and the Scandinavian countries including Iceland, and we should gladly welcome them. But going further than that into southern or eastern Europe, I should say that we have no room for immigration from these places. We have now in this country too many of these people whom we cannot properly assimilate. The United States has discovered to its cost what it meant to open its doors wide to southern and central Europe. That country has been called the melting pot of nations, and one of its humorous writers, Mr. George Ade, in an 88 '
article which I read some time ago, said that this idea of the United States having become the melting pot of nations must be forever cast aside. It was, he said, more properly designated a churn. I think there is perhaps more force in that remark than some of us may imagine at first. At any rate, when you pour into a melting pot metals of various kinds you can hardly expect that they will fuse and that the product will be refined gold or anything of great value. .
I am honestly concerned in the question as to the future of our Canadian West. I would gladly support any system that would possibly keep intact as much as possible in their purity of blood the two great races of this northern portion of the American continent. If we could retain as far as possible the purity of the French race, the race descended from the British stock and the people of northern Europe, we should be doing a great service to the future of this country. But if we allow, as has been done in the past, immigration to come in from among people who will not readily adapt themselves to our habits and customs, people whose racial peculiarities are, to say the least, not ours, I fear the time may come when we shall deplore the fact that we have been so generous in that respect in our immigration laws.
I have listened throughout this debate with no very great degree of pleasure, I must confess, to the somewhat doleful strains that have come from the members from the western provinces regarding the situation there. Now, I ought to have a very great amount of sympathy for the farming element in the West, for I suppose, unless I am mistaken, that I was in that country as a settler probably earlier than any man in this House. At all events, I was in Calgary in the spring of 1883, before the railroad reached that country, and I saw the first rush of settlers arrive in Alberta. I took up land there myself and attempted for two or three years to make a success of farming. However, whether through my own fault, or otherwise, I did not attain any degree of success in that province, and it was not long until I sought what I thought were conditions, climatic and otherwise, that would better suit me, and moved across the Rockies to British Columbia. And I have not greatly regretted that change. But I should sympathize with the difficulties which the prairie provinces have gone through; and I was glad to note that, after some distressing tales had been placed before the House by several members of that section of the country, a more optimistic and cheerful note was struck by the

134S
Supply-Immigration

member for Springfield and others who followed him. I am not one of those who views with any great deal of apprehension the future of that country. I come from a section of British Columbia where we have had great difficulties and passed through times of stress and strain, and the people are now suffering from severe depression. But hops springs high among them and there is a steady tendency to courage and optimism; and I know they would not thank me if in this House I gave expression to any particular apprehension regarding the future which awaits them in that really favoured section of the country. I believe therefore that we are justified in bidding our friends from the prairies to be of good cheer and hope. Times are mending, I believe, and much may be done for them and for other sections of the Dominion by the pursuit of a sane, sound and reasonable policy of immigration.
Taxation of course bears heavily on every portion of Canada. In addition to the very serious and, as some may say, alarming burden of national debt, every province is hampered with a very heavy burden of internal taxation. Municipal taxes are high; they are now higher perhaps by one hundred per cent than they were ten or fifteen years ago in most parts of Canada. So that the burden of taxation presses heavily on the shoulders of all. Now, in order to increase 10 p.m. our wealth and lessen that burden it seems to me it is absolutely necessary to have further production; and to bring about increased production it is equally necessary to increase our population. Our railways carry a heavy burden of debt and deficit which bears heavily on the finances of the Dominion, and we know that the only way that burden can be relieved is by giving the railways increased business; and, in turn, the only way that increased business can be secured is through an increased population. I confess that we are almost on the horns of a dilemma in this regard. When we consider the question of unemployment, which is assuming large proportions in several parts of the country, to bring in indiscriminate additions to the population might be to increase that evil considerably. But after weighing everything as well as one may in the balance, we must be forced to one conclusion or the other; and the conclusion I have reached is that the time is now come to begin a more vigorous policy of itamigration into this country than hitherto has been in force. I believe in my province. It is a province that has wonderful resources in the way of timber and mines and it has a vast 
coastal fisheries development, in connection with which more labour could be employed than is at present at work. I believe that in the industrial centres at least the time has come when more labour will be demanded; and I am sure that in all sections of Canada the time is here when more settlers can be found for the land.
I have no particular desire to protract the debate, which has already extended over a considerable time. But any time devoted to the discussion of this subject is, I think, well spent, for no more important question could engage the attention of parliament this session. While I cannot honestly congratulate the -minister upon all the details of the policy he has brought down before the House, I will give him credit for having made an attempt to solve the problem with which he is faced.
I am sure he has given the matter earnest consideration, and possibly before his estimates are passed he will revise some of his decisions, which, he has candidly told us, are not as inflexible as the laws of the Medes and Persians. The discussion this afternoon has given him, no doubt, occasion to pause and consider whether to go ahead with the policy he has outlined or to proceed along different lines. Speaking only for myself, I am in favour of a more generous measure of immigration than has hitherto been .effective in this country. The time has come when some of the restrictions which have been imposed may with safety be relaxed. We need more people on our land: in fact I believe that in nearly every sphere of activity more people will very shortly be required. I sincerely trust that before this discussion is concluded the minister will give serious consideration to some of the representations that have been made.

Mr. Chairman, the government went to a good deal of trouble this afternoon to justify the Western Canada Colonization Association and the stand they have taken behind it. But I do not believe that is the crux of the situation at all; what we should justly consider to-day is whether or not we should bring more people into Canada while those already here are having such a hard time to make a living. I do not think that the good faith of the government has been called into question, especially by the group of which I form a part. However, before entering upon a discussion of the question of immigration I would like to make a few remarks in regard to some statements that have been made by previous speakers-not with any intention of criticising them, but simply

Supply-Immigration
because they left the wrong impression upon the committee.
The other afternoon our colleague the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) dwelt largely upon the over-institutionalized condition of the western country. That condition may exist in Winnipeg, but it does not exist in many portions of the West. The hon. member spoke about the fine, big parliament buildings in Winnipeg. Of these I know very little, and I would not like to tell what I do know. Then he told about their schools and their churches. According to his story they have plenty of room, there being very few scholars in each room of their schools. That is not the condition further west. The member for Swift Current (Mr. Lewis) also referred to the schools, and he made it plain that in Saskatchewan, school room was not quite as abundant as it was in Manitoba. I could not help wondering if that was a progressive broadening out, starting in the east and increasing as it went west, because I assure the committee that by the time you get to Edmonton the schools are very much cramped. I am advised that there are 15,000 school children in that city, in 64 rooms, an average of 51 in each room. There are 17 rooms in the high school, with 933 students, an average of 54 in each room. Twenty-five of these rooms are contained in basements. I mention this simply -to show that if there is a large influx of people from outside, our provincial and municipal governments will have to spend considerable sums in order to provide the necessary facilities for them.
One hon. member made a remark about our scratching the ground out in the West. That is a very familiar remark; almost every speaker who does not know much about farming will fall into the same error. However, in this section of the House we could man quite a number of farms and put an experienced farmer on each one, and we could also man the pulpits of several churches and put an experienced preacher in each of those pulpits. But I doubt very much whether we would be well advised to start our farmers in the pulpits or to accept our preachers as authorities on agriculture. The West has proven itself time and again. We have produced big crops year after year-I am speaking of the West as a whole. I do not believe that the country can be criticised, or that the farmer can be criticised. During war years, when we were called upon for a large production, we furnished a production that surprised the world. The hon. member ended up with the statement that if we brought in other farmers to co-operate with us we would enjoy 861
greater prosperity than any other part of the country. About the time he was saying that, our special committee on Agriculture was taking evidence and a sworn witness was stating that flour was being shipped from the United States to England at a lower price than from Canada to England, and further that it was the intention of the transportation companies to raise the rate on cattle. I think it is now $20 and they anticipate putting it up to $25. A good deal of other evidence of a similar character was given. We shall never be a prosperous community so long as things are so arranged that when the price of grain goes up the elevator companies will take advantage of it and when the price of cattle goes up some transportation company will increase its charges and the farmer will get no benefit from the advance in price. If that is the prosperity that we nope to enjoy in Canada, it is of very doubtful quality indeed.
I would like also to make a few comments upon some of the statements made by the minister when he was explaining to the committee his colonization undertaking. Speaking the other afternoon, he said that conditions were worse now than they were in 1892. Well, I do not see how it is possible to compare conditions now with those prevailing at that time; things have changed very considerably since then. For instance, in 1892 there was only a small amount of debt in the world, and that was particularly true of this country. It was a simple matter for everyone to make a living in those days. Your necessary expenditure was very low, and if a man was out of employment for several months or for any considerable time, he would not get greatly involved. To-day it is wholly different; when you get up in the morning you know that you must make several dollars before night in order to pay essential expenses. If for any reason a man's income is suspended for a little while, his overhead expenses will rapidly eat up a considerable amount of money. The minister further stated that twenty-five to thirty per cent of the settlers will be able to establish themselves when they come to this country. I am very sorry that he did not tell us from what country those settlers were coming. I do not believe you could point to any of the European countries at least that is sending out settlers who will be able to establish themselves when they get here.
His next statement was that from fifteen to twenty-five per cent of our western farmers were already in bankruptcy, that from fifteen to twenty-five per cent more are in a serious condition, and that many more are not on
Supply-Immigration

Easy street. Well, I would suggest that that probably means that in his estimation about half of the farmers are in bankruptcy or very close to it. Now it requires a long stretch of the imagination to think that these farmers the minister is going to bring out from Europe, who are unacquainted with farming conditions in our western country, who have little or no money save the SI,500 or $2,000 which I think was the amount he suggested, could establish themselves on, can go on the farms which our experienced farmers have gone into bankruptcy trying to operate, and make good. I ask you, hon. gentlemen, is there any prospect in this world of them making good?
Then he stressed the fact that three months ago the only workers we could consider bringing into this country were those who would engage in agriculture. But to-day that policy is changed, and we can admit some other classes. However, he advanced no argument whatever to show that conditions had bettered in Canada in the meantime, only that conditions had bettered in the United States, and that they had drawn part of our population there, and we could bring in others to take their place.
The question was asked, why the government always advertised the prairie lands. Why did they not leave some immigrants down through old Ontario and Quebec? The minister very frankly stated that it was because the natural resources of the prairie provinces were still held by the Dominion government, and they had been exploiting the western lands. I wonder if the government ever think that the day is not liable to come when an accounting will have to be given for these western lands which they have been exploiting. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) speaking the other night made the statement that this government had spent about $30,000,000 in bringing immigrants into Canada, and that they had not an immigrant to show for it. The Prime Minister has spoken since that time, the Acting Minister of Immigration and several members of the government, but not one of them has attempted to refute that statement. Personally, I should like to know whether it is true or not. If it is not true, I should think it was up to the government to disprove it. We who sit in this portion of the House have been frankly criticised as calamity howlers. They tell us that we are stressing this condition, that we are over-drawing it. I do not think that we are worse than the rest. I have in my hand here a paper called The Mirror. I understand it is a new paper starting out on a very youthful career. On the
[Mr. Kellner. 1
front page is a picture of the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen). It is a very fine picture too, surrounded with a border of maple leaves.
It looks like a mourning band.

It is a picture his supporters may well be proud of. In fact, I expect to see it framed and hung probably in their offices in this building. On page 2 of that paper.I find this statement:
One farmer who in 1919 had a surplus of $28,000 without liabilities was now offering to sell his equity for $1,000 to secure enough money to leave the country	 Some grain shipped by the carload did not pay the freight.
I am very sorry the last speaker has left the chamber. He was one of those who stressed our calamity howling, but I do not think we have ever made it stronger than that. There is no question but that these conditions do exist, and it would be foolish to deceive ourselves and try to make out that they do not. If that statement I have read proves anything it simply proves this, that western Canada is a country where achievement and advancement can be made if we have a chance; else that man would not have had the $28,000. It also proves that certain well established arrangements have been made to separate him from any surplus money he gets from the opportunities he has.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: May I ask where this gentleman's farm is located that is mentioned in that interesting paper?

I shall be very glad to see that the minister gets a copy of the paper. I think the address is given, but I am not quite sure.
In my opinion there is not a member of this House who is opposed to immigration under favourable conditions, but we would do well to seriously consider whom we are liable to get if we embark on a policy of immigration at the present time. Most assuredly if we get the immigrant whom England and the European countries would like to see us get, we would get the present inhabitant of the bread line. That is the class they would like to send to us. We would also get the man who has probably been broken by the war, or the man who has found his occupation ruined by the war. He is more or less of a misfit. Another thing we will find when he comes to this country, undoubtedly he will have a lot more dependents than the like number of immigrants coming to this country ever had before. Most assuredly in a war where the

Supply-Immigration
t
majority of the young and strong men have been lost, those who are not able to work for a living will depend upon the remainder to work for them, and if we bring them out to this country we can expect their dependents to come with them. One thing we can be sure of and that is that the adventurous, the strong young man, the man who used to be our ideal immigrant, will not come in very large numbers at this time.
Probably the next matter for our consideration is what shall we do with him when we get him here? I understand that if this government policy goes through, it will be their aim to put these people on the land at considerable expense, and they will keep them there for a while. After a while, when men find out that they are up against a hopeless proposition, they will leave the farms. Some will go to the cities, and some will probably migrate to some other country. It is evidently the policy of this government to have an ever changing farm population. We will have one group of men from time to time moving off the farms, and we will be going over to Europe to get another group to come and take their places. There can be no stability whatever in agriculture under those conditions.
I think we might well stop and consider the spirit of these immigrants who are leaving our country. Let me picture to you what, to my mind might take place in some of those homes. The husband and the wife no doubt will meet in consultation. For months they have been considering ways and means which might enable them to keep going. Hope is fast sinking and finally it disappears. All this time the children have been eager listeners to their conversation. They leave our country and probably go to a foreign land. They make new friends and new acquaintances, and when these new acquaintances come to visit them and find that they have come from Canada, undoubtedly the conversation will again revert to this Dominion, and those children who were bom upon our land and were in their early youth citizens of mu' country, will once more hear reproaches heaped upon this Dominion which gave them birth. I ask you, in all sincerity, do you think it is fitting that we should allow our people to leave our country and our young people especially to receive such lessons as that?
I think there are unquestionably two immigration policies before the people of Canada to-day. One is a policy which declares, although agriculture is in an impoverished condition: We will establish a certain number of farmers and we will keep them on those farms as long as we can; and when the task
becomes hopeless they will leave and we will get another group to take their place. Ever changing and ever shifting we will go from one strata of society to another until eventually we will reach the lowest. The other policy contemplates a prosperous farming community, and that is what the group that sits in this corner of the chamber considers we are entitled to. We are convinced that if a man works ten, twenty, thirty or forty years on a farm and saves his money he should, at least, be entitled to a home to live in and a few hundred dollars besides.
In any other line but fanning, when production exceeds the demand it is always considered good business to limit that production. For instance, out in the province where I live we produce a large amount of coal, and it is not an unusual thing at all to see a newspaper editorial advising the coal mine operators that the mines have the capacity of producing far more coal than there is any prospect of the market consuming. So the editorial would say "It would be a matter of good business for you operators to get together and decide on the amount of your production, because if you go ahead and produce without any regard to markets you will stall the thing and you are bound to lose money". That ought to be a good business policy for agriculture also. On the other hand they say to the farmers "You go out and produce every bushel that you can, raise every hoof that you can, and the Lord, in some unseen way, will provide a market for you". If I am any judge of conditions I would very seriously recommend that we go slowly in increasing our production at the present time. I would like any advocate of increased production to show me what country is in a position to buy our goods unless we are prepared to take the goods which they produce. Most assuredly there is no European country to-day that can afford to buy largely from us unless we are in a position to re-buy from them. And what do we do? We erect a good big tariff wall around our country and keep their goods out. It is a hopeless proposition: If we will not let their goods in most assuredly they cannot buy ours.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I would like to suggest to this government that instead of spending this money trying to induce people to come here they would be justified in making an earnest effort to first put our people who are now engaged in agriculture on their feet, and there is a real opportunity to accomplish something along this line at the present time. I do not think there ever was a time in the history of the country when the agriculturists
i
Supply-Immigration

had the entire sympathy of the rest of the Dominion to the extent they have to-day. I believe that if the government would take the money it is proposed to grant to the Western Canada Colonization Association and with it go out and try to organize some form of marketing societies, that would look after the home market at any rate, they could do a real service. It seems to me, let me say here, the height of folly that the price of the wheat that we use in producing flour in Canada should be set in Liverpool. I never could quite understand why, if a miller somewhere in Ontario wished to buy a carload of western wheat he had to cable to Liverpool to find out how much that wheat was worth. I do not think there is any question but that au effort of the kind I have indicated would at least stabilize our home market. I have in my office a little booklet called, I think, Four thousand facts about Canada which states that 80 per cent of our production is used at home. I am not sure that that proportion is right, but it would not surprise me at all if it were. However, whether that proportion be right or not there is a large volume of it used here in Canada. It has been sold away under the cost of production; and if this government had the welfare of the farmers at heart they would be well advised to seriously considering something that would stabilize the home market.
In discussing this immigration policy the arguments which have been advanced so far in favour of bringing in immigrants, I think, to say the least, are very heartless. One of them-I do not know whether an hon. member actually said it or whether it just occurred , to me-was that, "Misery loves company." I think it probably is the most impressive argument of all. The next one, and probably the one which is the most advanced, is that it is going to build up our railroads. I believe it is the first time any country, that claims agriculture as its basic industry has made the statement that agriculture should be made subservient to industry. If farming is our basic industry most assuredly it should not be made subservient to the railroads or to any other industry. Then we are told that a vigorous immigration policy and the bringing in of more people will help us to pay our debts; and over in Europe they say "If we could only get rid of our surplus population our debts would not bother us so much." This argument is identical with that upon which the tariff policy is based; I do not think it is necessary to stress it at all.
In conclusion I would call the attention of the House to the fact that the policy which has been laid down by the government is very
I Mr. Kellner.]
similar, in many ways, to the old policy which was in force down in the southern states about half a century or more ago. They tell us that they will bring in immigrants and put them on the farms mortgaged to the hilt. For the next thirty-two years-we can say forty years because they will have four or five failures in that time-they will be busy paying the interest and trying to keep out of debt and in the meantime we will have the Soldier Settlement Board supervising their operations and keeping watch over them. Mr. Chairman, is it not very similar to what they did in slavery days in the south? It is true the system is gone; they no longer buy and sell human beings. Yes, the slave is gone, the black snake is gone, but the spirit is there-the spirit of slavery; and I do not believe, if you bring these people in and load them down with a debt such as is proposed, that there is any prospect whatever of their ever getting out of debt in forty years' time: Think of the attractive life which is before them. Every morning when they wake up they will know that through that day they will have to toil In order to get sufficient to pay the interest on their debts. I think it is the most hopeless outlook that any people could be asked to accept. For my part, I intend to vote against the resolution, and I hope this government will yet change its intention and decide on something at least a little more human.

In rising to state my tale of woe in connection with this debate, I want to say I have followed the speeches delivered by hon. members from the beginning with much interest. My impression is that some of the speeches delivered here have been far-fetched, yes, almost weird. In this connection I recall the speecch delivered by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion), when he said that if Canada was to have free trade, the East must die. We heard the speech of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie;, who told us about the streams of gold going to the United States and contended that the tariff should be placed higher and yet higher. We also heard the viewpoint of labour as expressed by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Irvine), who told us that he was not in sympathy with bringing immigrants into Canada so long as there were many unemployed in our cities. If these statements mean anything, they mean that these hon. gentlemen advocate the continuance of a policy of exploitation, the same policy we have had in Canada for forty years, a policy the monumental stupidity of which has placed

S upply-I mmigration
a blight upon Canadian agriculture and has retarded national development.
But, Mr. Chairman, I do not rise to deal with tariff or streams of gold or unemployment. To my mind the question of immigration must go hand in hand with the land policy of the Dominion. I believe that experience has demonstrated that the whole question of immigration is closely related to that of land settlement. That is the particular question I wish to deal with this evening. It is my intention to endeavour to make a survey of immigration and Dominion land policies in the past, to endeavour, if possible, to point out the mistakes that have been made, to suggest how these mistakes may be corrected, and to express the hope that we may benefit by this knowledge in laying down our immmigration and land policies for the future. We heard about the prosperity of the province of Manitoba, and I was very glad to hear it, but I recall in studying the early history of Manitoba, that previous to the eighties and nineties the industry of agriculture in Manitoba was in a very precarious condition indeed. As a matter of fact, western agriculture never was put on a proper basis until the discovery of the summer-fallow system of tillage. The discovery of the summer-fallow system of tillage was the signal for a tremendous improvement in the prosperity of western Canada, generally, but particularly the province of Manitoba and the eastern part of the province of Saskatchewan. The soil of the province of Manitoba and the soil of eastern Saskatchewan was found admirably adapted to the summer-fallow method, and as a result of that there came the development of agriculture to the westward.
In those days there were many millions of acres of Dominion lands in western Canada. Prior to 1908 I believe 32,000,000 acres of land were given in grants to the railway companies, and about 32,000,000 acres homesteaded. About the year 1908 the government changed their policy in regard to Dominion lands in western Canada. It was decided about that time to discontinue the policy of making grants of lands to railway companies, and because the Hudson Bay railway was then in contemplation it was decided to sell certain lands in the southwestern part of Saskatchewan and southern Alberta, in order to realize enough money to push that road through to Hudson bay. During those years the progress of our railway development was to the westward; as the branch lines extended to the westward, settlement followed the railways. We find that the railways selected in the main the choice land. They did not at that time select much land in the southwestern part of Saskatchewan or southern Alberta. The lands were selected along the northern section, and settlement followed the railways. About the time the Dominion Lands Act was passed in 1908 an area was set aside in southwestern Saskatchewan and southern Alberta, consisting of approximately 28,000,000 acres. Whether it was because of the fact that the railway companies had not selected lands within that area or not, I am not prepared to say, but at any rate there was a general feeling at that time that southwestern Saskatchewan and southern Alberta were not adapted to the industry of agriculture. Stock raising was encouraged in that district at that time. As a matter of fact, the stock raising industry gained considerable dimensions during those years. The Dominion Lands Act in 1908 was the signal for a tremendous inrush of settlement to the pre-emption area. Many of the settlers came from the Old Land and many also from the United States. In the years between 1908 and 1915 or 1916 many thousand immigrants came in from the United States and settled on those lands. Just here I would like to say, in connection with the question I am trying to deal with, that I have not gleaned my knowledge of it from reading departmental reports. I have passed through the experience of homesteading in that area, and in 1908 I also acquired a preemption.
At the time of the amendment of the Dominion Lands Act in 1908, the Hon. Frank Oliver, who was then Minister of the Interior, recognized the fact that within that area more land was necessary to constitute the average farm because of unfavourable climatic and soil conditions. In that country there is not as heavy an annual rainfall as there is in the province of Manitoba or in eastern Saskatchewan, and we find, if we look over the debates at the time of the passing of the Dominion Lands Act, that this was used as an argument why the pre-emption privilege should be extended to that area. There was one feature however which the Dominion Lands Act of 1908 did not recognize, and it was the fact that within that large area while there are many lands which are absolutely unsuited for tillage purposes, there are many thousands of acres of probably as choice land as you will find in the Dominion of Canada. I would say roughly that within that area the amount of choice land might be about 30 per cent. Then, perhaps, another 30 per cent of the land might be considered as fair, and probably 40 per cent of it might be considered as absolutely unsuited for tillage purposes. The latter lands have an-
Supply-Imviigra tion

other use, namely for grazing purposes, and some of them have been used in that way.
The great mistake of the Dominion Lands Act of 1908 was in failing to recognize that fact. The land, the good and the bad, was thrown open indiscriminately, and because of the inrush of immigrants at that time, and the demand for free lands, all those lands were taken up and settled. After 1908, and prior to possibly 1916 or 1917, there was a period of marked prosperity. The years 1917, 1918 and 1919 were very dry years, and it was not until those years that the fact became apparent that there were within that area many lands which were not adapted for tillage purposes. In 1920, the provincial government of Saskatchewan, which has ever been alive to the necessities of agriculture in that province, instituted an inquiry into the deplorable state of agriculture in that part of the province. The result of the inquiry was the appointment of a commission to investigate conditions generally, and it was found that the great mistake as regards that area was the throwing open for settlement of lands which should have been kept closed, that is, which should have been used entirely for grazing purposes.
Just at this point let me say that over 14,000,000 acres of land have been sold within that area as pre-emptions and purchased homesteads between 1908 and the present time. The total revenue received from the sale of such pre-emptions and purchased homesteads, within the pre-emption area up to the present time, is aproximately $19,000,000. In 1922, the total revenue received from the sale of pre-emptions and purchased homesteads within that area was but $350,000, notwithstanding the fact that outstanding obligations by virtue of pre-emptions and purchased homesteads within that area are approximately $12,000,000 at the present time. The situation which we have been faced with within that area since 1918 is this, that on those poorer areas which I mentioned, after the first crop or two, when the humus was removed from the soil, the soil commenced to drift, to blow, and consequently our people began to move out. The people were driven off those lands, and many of them went to the States. Also from the lands which I stated were good to fair, there is a movement of population as well. Many of the remaining settlers find it impossible or next to impossible to continue on those lands; but notwithstanding this, the department are demanding from them the full payment of their pre-emption obligations, in spite of the fact that most of those obligations have now been running from eight to ten years.
[Mr McTaggart.l
One of the recommendations of the commission which the Saskatchewan government appointed, was the establishment of community pastures within that area. It was their recommendation that the small rancher farmer should be encouraged. The growing of grain exclusively within that area, it is felt, will not be found profitable. The profitable farm in that area, in the future as in the past, will be that of the farmer who has access to grazing lands. If there is a section or a half section of grazing land near a settler's farm, and if he could have access to that land for grazing purposes for his stock, that would be of great advantage. Where there are grazing areas too . large for the private leaseholder, it is felt that such areas should be taken advantage of by settlers adjoining the area and used as community pastures. I hope the minister is familiar with the recommendations of the commission in that regard. As a matter of fact, I believe the department is familial with the recommendations because, as I understand the matter, any large leaseholds which are to be thrown open in the near future in that district, are to be leased to the provincial government, in the expectation that the latter government will re-lease to associations of settlers, so that they may form community pastures.
As regards the exodus from that area, the figures which I have and which were brought down in the House, I believe, about two weeks ago, go to show that during 1922, 842 quarter sections, pre-emptions and purchased homesteads, were either cancelled or abandoned. So, we see from that the process of depopulation which is going on. The situation as we see it is that the department is forced from time to time to try to collect overdue obligations on those pre-emptions and purchased homesteads, and in this way the department is actually acting the part of driving those people out of the country.

We are not insisting and have not, since I have been in office, insisted on the settlement of payments on pre-emptions, hoping to give the individual every opportunity. But I would like to point out to my hon. friend that $16,000,000 have been paid in on pre-emptions, and the situation is a rather difficult one, inasmuch as all the pre-emptions which represent the payment of $16,000,000 have been paid for in full. To adopt a policy now to begin to readjust payments on pre-emptions would not be fair to those who are paid up. We are not, however, pressing for payment.

I desire to thank the minister for the explanation. As a matter of fact, I was aware that of recent months there have not been as many letters going to holders of pre-emptions and purchased homesteads. The situation is one that we must face in the near future. What is to be done? Those payments have been running along now for many years, and although the extensions from time to time help us to stave off the day when this situation will have to be met, yet I feel that a complete survey of conditions there is very necessary, so that we may be able to clear up the unfortunate situation which exists in that area.
Some reference has been made to the blacklisting of this particular area. The area has been blacklisted to a certain extent. I believe some of the settlers in that area have been as much responsible as anyone else for that blacklisting; but as a matter of fact, the Department of the Interior have recognized that certain sections within that area are of an inferior quality, for they have withdrawn certain sections entirely from homestead entry. There are other areas within which restrictions have been placed upon homestead entry.
Now, the lesson which I think we might learn from the unfortunate situation in the southwest is that there should be, in the case of free lands thrown open for settlement, a classification of lands with a view to setting aside those areas not considered fit for agricultural purposes. And while I am not familiar with the areas of free lands which we have left in Canada, yet I am inclined to believe that we may have a situation similar to that which existed in the southwest. I feel confident to-day that had there been in 1908 a classification of lands in southwestern Saskatchewan and southern Alberta, and had those areas which were thought not fit for tillage purposes been set aside and withdrawn from entry, we should not have the unfortunate conditions which we have in the southwest at the present time. The result has been a hardship on the settlers on the good soil within that area; because when the settlers on the poorer soils were compelled to move out they left a burden of taxation in the shape of school and municipal taxes, the gravity of which I am sure all hon. members will be able to understand. The people who departed left an indebtedness by virtue of school taxes, telephone taxes and municipal taxes, which are adding to the burden on those who are left.
We have heard something about the burdens which agriculture has had to bear. As I mentioned at the outset, I am of the opinion
that the tariff is one of the heaviest burdens which we have to bear now and in the past. But it is not the only burden. The burden of labour itself has borne very heavily on agriculture. The hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) told us this evening about how the farmers in the past had exploited labour. I am going to analyse this statement from the standpoint of the farmer. In 1905 I worked in the harvest fields at Indian Head in Saskatchewan, and at that time the average wage was $1.75 per day. The total cost of operating an average sized threshing machine in 1905, a machine with a capacity of say 2,000 bushels a day, was $62 per day; that is to say, the average labour cost, not taking into account repairs, or teams, or overhead, interest, depreciation, oil, fuel, or anything of that kind. I am referring entirely to direct labour cost. In 1915 I had an interest in a threshing machine in the district in which I live, so that I know whereof I speak, and in that year the wage had risen to $3.50 a day on the average in the harvest fields; while the total labour cost of the same sized machine as that I mentioned previously would be in 1915 approximately $95 per day. In 1922, I was still operating the same machine which I operated in 1915, and we find the labour cost in the year 1922 to be $160 a day, with wages from $6 to $7 a day. This certainly was not an exploitation of labour. Now, I want to know if any hon. member in this House will say that we do not need immigration of agricultural labourers into Canada. Since I have been in western Canada I have never known the time when there has been an over-supply of agricultural labourers. Perhaps at times in certain communities there has been a surplus, but to my knowledge, there has never been any time when there has been an over-supply of such labour.
We heard the statement the last day this subject was under discussion that one of the troubles with farming in western Canada was that the farms were too large. To me that statement is a very misleading one, because I fancy that after all the size of farms in any country must be controlled more or less by conditions of location, soil and climate. In this connection I wish to quote a few words from the report of the commission which the Saskatchewan government appointed in 1920 in regard to this matter, as applied to southwestern Saskatchewan. This is what the report says:
Indeed it seems to your commissioners that unless range is found in more or less extensive blocks for community grazing the size of the farms in the southwest

will have to be substantially larger than a half section in order to provide facilities for grazing.
Let me read in this connection the point of view of the Hon. Mr. Oliver himself as expressed in 1908 in reference to lands in the southwest. I quote from Hansard of 1908 at page 11142:
Now, we believe that would be a very great deterrent to settlement in that part of the country. We believe that the conditions there, being such as I have described, a 320 acre farm is one of fair average size and means should be offered to new settlers to acquire such a farm, He cannot acquire it from the railway company, because the railway company is not there; the lands are in the hands of the government to-day, and the government is the only person with whom the settler can deal.
Now, we have heard much preaching about patriotism and unity, both in and out of this House, and I think the time is ripe for us to get down to something practical in connection with these professions. I am going to relate to this House the case of an immigrant who came to Canada about the year 1912, a British boy from the Old Country about 21 or 22 years of age. This young fellow, Harry Dawes, filed a homestead and pre-emption in 1912 or 1913, in the territory of which I have spoken. In 1914 he was in my employ when the war broke out, and shortly after the declaration of hostilities this young Britisher, who was an energetic boy, joined the colours and went
11 p.m. overseas with the first contingent.
He went across to France and was killed in action on the 24th of May, 1915. He left a widowed mother in the Old Land and to this day she has not been able to dispose of that pre-emption in Saskatchewan. I have a letter from the administrator of the estate which came just a few weeks ago and I am going to read from it a paragraph or two. He says:
My point is this. The soldier who returned from the war was allowed to transfer his pre-emption to a soldier grant, meaning that he got it free. Surely the soldier who gave his life for this country earned equally as much as the returned man.
I took the question up with the department, but they could not do anything more than extend the time of the payment due on the pre-emption. I have no fault to find with the department; I wish to make that clear, but I feel that in this case injustice has been done.
As I stated at the beginning, I did not tell the story of, the southwest with the idea of enlisting the sympathy of parliament for that part of the country; my object was to ensure that we should derive from the mistakes of the past something that might be of benefit to us in developing the new lands we expect to settle in the future. I am in favour of

immigration of agricultural labour into Canada. I am in favour of the immigration of British and Scandinavian labour. I will try to sum up the observations I have made by offering the following recommendations:
1.	That encouragement be given the immigration of British and Scandinavian workers with the view of ensuring a steady flow of desirable agricultural labourers for the farms of Canada.
2.	That a thorough classification of all Dominion lands be undertaken by competent authority with a view of arranging for the disposition of these lands in a way which shall ensure the maximum of agricultural production, the greatest conservation of soil resources, and the utmost prosperity for the largest possible population.
3.	That the minister give earnest consideration to the advisability of cancelling outstanding pre-emption and purchased homestead obligations with a view of arresting the unfortunate exodus of settlers from the preemption area.
4.	That a thorough survey of the whole question of Crown land administration be carried out at an early date with a view of incorporating the recommendations of such survey in the long overdue revision of the Dominion Lands Act.
In conclusion, I have only this to say: if the minister earnestly desires to do some colonization work in Canada he might profitably turn his attention to the southwest, because in that district he could work in the way of correcting past mistakes that would be of great benefit not only to the West but to the whole of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, this question which has now been discussed for a considerable time, has been well presented to the committee by hon. members from this corner. When I first came to this House four years ago I presented the case of the agriculturists; on many occasions I stated that I did not think due consideration had been given on the floor of parliament to the agriculturists throughout the Dominion. I was the subject of criticism on the part of hon. members, on the ground that I was an alarmist, but to-day all will agree that if at that time I was a missionary sent down here I have since been followed by a goodly number of "alarmists" who have told the same story that I tried to tell in 1920 -the story of actual conditions pertaining to agriculture in our western country. The Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) know that the conditions outlined by speakers

Supply-Immigration
in this debate actually exist. I firmly believe that the Minister of Immigration is doing what he believes best, perhaps, for all of Canada, but I also believe that upon his own initiative he would not advance this proposal. I do not wish my remarks to be interpreted as a criticism of the minister, for I sympathize greatly with him in his endeavour to arrive at a solution of this problem. But I doubt very much whether the solution is to be found through this western colonization scheme.
It has been stated on numerous occasions in this House that there is a leak in our immigration policy. Men and women leave our country after being brought here, and' if , money must be spent, it should be used to stop that leak. And what will stop it? Nothing more nor less than the making of conditions pertaining to agriculture what they should be. Speaking of the minister's attitude on this question, I have in my hand a reference which states:
Hon. Charles Stewart, Minister of the Interior and Acting Minister of Immigration for Canada, in open frankness, speaking before the University Club at Ottawa, recently stated:
"The market at home is overstocked with, produce, which cannot be sold profitably because of the high overhead of those doing business. Thte is the result of deflation in some lines and not in others. Particularly affected by those conditions is the farmer. Extreme conditions of deflation in the farming communities of the West have resulted in the impossibility of making the farms pay there. What is the use of bringing people to this country if they cannot exist?"
No truer word has been spoken in this House or in any other assembly than those words uttered by the Acting Minister of Immigration. That, in my estimation, is the real thought that permeates the mind of the minister; he is so well advised regarding agricultural conditions in western Canada that he knows that an immigration policy based upon this principle cannot, of necessity, be successful. After thirty-two years' experience in western Canada I should know something about agricultural conditions there. I have seen many ups and downs in a national way; more have I seen from the individual standpoint. I recollect in the early days the possibility of a person going out, starting up and making headway. It is true that there were many evils in those days, but we fought them and persuaded the powers that be to legislate so that we could overcome them. In that connection I wish to compliment the minister in that he did, when connected with the government of Alberta, rectify many of the evils from which agriculturists suffered. I recall the days when we were not privileged to order a car to ship our grain but were obliged to shoot it through a hole in
the side of an elevator. These things, and the principle of co-operation, we have brought about by agitation and by getting the ear of the government. I state that here at this present time in this Dominion parliament we likewise who represent agriculture should have the ears of the government. We maintain that we who do understand agricultural conditions in the West have a right to be heard. We are just as good in the giving of evidence as the Western Canada Colonization Association. I maintain that these gentlemen who are so philanthropic might better go out themselves and demonstrate the possibilities of agriculture in the West, than ask this government to provide them with a percentage to carry on their work of bringing in immigrants. It does seem to me that we have a right to be heard. No one can doubt our sincerity. No one will accuse us of wilfully making statements that have not been corroborated by evidence submitted.
I wish to state- that I am in favour of immigration. I do not wish my remarks to be interpreted as disapproving of immigration. But I do not believe in the principle of patrimony or patronage. I remember so well when I was a small boy my father migrating from Hampshire in England and bringing out his family and establishing them without a dollar of assistance in the county of Lambton in Ontario. As his boys grew up they moved westward, and I am proud to say that each and every one of them has made a very fair success. Conditions were better then, but I would point out that no patronage and no patrimony was given, and I think we were proud enough to say that if it had been offered we would not have accepted it. We were prepared and willing to take our chances, and we did take our chances and whatever we became, the credit can be given to ourselves and to our upbringing. Thousands of others went into western Canada who to-day after long years of experience and effort may have a little equity, but thousands and thousands who have come in later under different conditions are finding it absolutely impossible to make a start upon land. They simply cannot do it, and their hearts are broken in a very few years. That is what will happen when you bring in settlers under this immigration scheme. Three years will be a sufficient length of time to break the heart of the immigrant who comes in under this scheme, and the government will find thousands of immigrants coming into the country as a result of this policy. What are we going to do then? Will the government assume another burden of debt? Will these

lands be capitalized and another petition be made to the people of Canada, and another effort made to bring more immigrants into the country and settle on the land? I think that possibly that will be the only solution then.
If you will trace the history of governments at the present time in parts of the world where white people obtain and are engaged in agriculture, Australia, for instance, we find there that the people are lamenting, almost weeping because of the condition to which agriculture has been brought. In Great Britain we find that the same conditions obtain. Go to any civilized country in the world and you will find agriculture bleeding to death, the whole world over. Agriculture's successes are built on agriculture's failures. By that I mean that if we in this country have a good crop and some other country in the world has a poor crop, we have a proportionate advantage, and likewise the other country when conditions are the reverse. So agriculture's successes are based on agriculture's failures. We compete with the world. As Mr. J. J. Morrison says in an article:
Labour to-day has better homes, better wages while we are at a standstill. Every jail farm in the country is in direct competition with your industry, but you do not object.
Such is the case with agriculture. I do not presume to argue that this government has the means to legislate against such conditions as that. Moreover, I do not think that agriculture is asking for any patrimony or patronage. But I ask this on behalf of agriculture, that when all the interests of Canada, and I care not what institution it is, have through all these years been showing in their anunal returns a dividend-I demand the same privilege for agriculture. I am prepared to take a one per cent dividend on my capitalization if that is sufficient for these other interests, but when they declare a ten or a fifteen per cent dividend, I ask for the same privilege for agriculture. I am not prepared to accept the position that they year after year shall declare a dividend of ten or twelve or fifteen per cent, and just leave me what is left, because I have had a very interesting part in the production of the wealth upon which their dividends are declared. That is only a square deal to all concerned, and surely, in stressing that point we are not asking for too much.
I was particularly interested in the remarks that were made by the hon. member for Springfield in the address which he gave the other day, and I wish to make a few references to them. The hon. member pointed out that in Manitoba, of which he presumed to speak with authority, they were over-

institutionalized, which is very true. In fact, all the grievances he mentioned were of provincial origin, but I would point out respectfully that the things which he cited were an added burden to the things we are debating at this time. We know full well of the over-institutionalism that has taken place in the western provinces, but in this federal House of Commons we have other problems, and I think it was quite beside the argument for the hon. gentleman to make those statements. His solution of the problem was to place cottages at a valuation of 82,400 on farms. That seemed to me to be something that carried us further, placing on us another burden similar to that placed upon us by Kaiser Bill when he declared war in 1914. I have made a little calculation here, and as the hon. member for Springfield spoke for Manitoba, I shall leave that province to him and take Saskatchewan and Alberta. I find that we have in those two provinces approximately 280,000 farms, which at $2,400 for a cottage, would amount to $712,000,000. That is the solution the hon. member for Springfield has for conditions in the West. I would ask hon. gentlemen of this House if they do not think I have enterprise enough myself to build a necessary house or cottage on my farm if conditions warrant it, and if conditions warrant it, by what means and in what manner I choose to do it. Am I to be told to accept a loan and to place this building on my land? That is not a solution. It only exaggerates the problem, makes it worse. Bid what surprised me most of all was that the hon. gentleman had departed from the stand that he took a year ago, and in that connection I wish to quote a paragraph from his budget address of last year. First let me say in passing that no gentleman from this part of the House spoke as earnestly about the conditions of agriculture in the West or more truthfully than did the hon. member for Springfield last year, when he said:
So burden after burden was added until I am sometimes afraid, although I trust I am mistaken, that we have added the last straw so far as western Canada is concerned. I have no desire to be unduly pessimistic, but I wonder if we are not living in a fool's paradise when we speak of western Canada and its ability to come back, unless we have a complete reversal of policy in this country.
Those were his sentiments only last year, and I wonder what has brought about the change, so that when he took his seat the other day he sat down amid applause from the government side while the best sentiment in the Progressive group sat silent and sullen. The hon. gentleman spoke

of prosperous conditions in Manitoba. He also said that he had been in this country fourteen years. I desire to state that I have been in Canada thirty-two years, and long before the hon.. member for Springfield was in Canada I trailed across the Riding mountains in a buckboard. I also forded rivers and streams and went into northern Manitoba looking out for suitable land. I stood upon that buckboard while it drifted down the stream but I got across eventually; there were no bridges in those days. I saw 500 of those immigrants who have been spoken of as successful to-day standing in the river stark naked bathing and washing. I went 300 miles further and I saw women hitched to the plough. I actually saw women drawing the plough in that territory in northern Manitoba. Those are the people the hon. gentleman described as being successful settlers. That is true, but the generations that have succeeded the people of those days are to-day in our agricultural colleges, and in our universities, and they are beating our own people in those institutions. But I want to ask the hon. gentleman whether he would ask the progeny of the members of this House- whether they live in the West or whether they live here-to go out there and compete with those people. I do not think, when you come down to realities, that we have got to work under such conditions to make agriculture a success. I do not believe, Sir, that those people could go into that same territory today and make a success of agriculture. Concerning the statements made by the hon. member it did seem to me that his whole argument was nothing but paternalism. I maintain that if conditions are right to-day that people can still go into our western country, with its potentialities, and make a success of farming. The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) also discussed the problem and his solution was to have industrial centres in the West where our products could be absorbed. The argument recalled to me the days when I went to school and used to read the verse:
There's a good time coming boys,
A good time coming.
We may not live to see the day,
But earth shall glisten in the ray
Of the good time coming.
I want-after spending my life in an effort to produce something that I might leave to posterity, after spending my life working earnestly and vigorously-to see these good times arrive in my own lifetime. My father hoped to live to see them, I also hope to see them, and it is but a poor consolation for the hon. member to simply assure us that there
is a good time coming. We are going to have a good time some day. We will have it all the quicker, I honestly believe, if the members of the government, will only hearken to the members in this corner of the chamber who have spoken in this debate, and endeavour to do something to remedy the evils from which agriculture is suffering. Those evils are economic, there is no question about it; and they are contributed to by interests of a predatory kind. That is where the trouble lies, I believe. There are individuals back of the Canada Colonization scheme who desire to have more people located on the lands throughout the West in order that they may climb upon their backs. Apparently they are on the backs of the people at the present . time and we ask them to get off, rather than bring in more people so that they may continue their present operation. These may perhaps seem harsh words, but I am absolutely in earnest. I believe I know whereof I speak and when I believe a thing I have no hesitation in giving expression to that belief.
I have a few figures here that I wish to submit; I know them so well that I believe I could almost quote them from memory. The provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta were formerly known as the Northwest Territories. In 1898 the population of Manitoba and the Northwest Territories was approximately 400,000 people; in 1922 approximately 2,000,000 people. In 1898 the wheat production in the area known as the Northwest Territories was 32,000,000 bushels. In 1922 the production of wheat in that same area amounted to 375,000,000 bushels. In the period from 1898 to 1922 the population increased five times in what is now our western provinces; whilst the production of wheat increased approximately eleven times. And yet the farmers to-day, taking man for man, are poorer than the settlers were in that early period, although the production of wheat is so vastly in excess of the increase in population. We may well ask what the reason is for the existing situation. When one looks at these figures, and they are official, one can readily understand why hon. members in this part of the chamber deem it incumbent upon them to state the facts.
It has occurred to me that if copies of Hansard for the past week were distributed throughout the countries from which we hope to draw immigrants it would be quite enlightening; particularly if an individual received the copies of Hansard at the same time as he received the publications issued by the Western Canada Colonization Association, or even the literature sent forward by the

present and previous governments. It would certainly be illuminating and yet I doubt whether we would accept the statements appearing in Hansard as facts.
From whence do we hope to attract immigrants? There is a difference of opinion in Great Britain at the present time as to whether the number of unemployed is 1,300,000 or 1,500,000. Ex-Premier Lloyd George accepts the latter figure. A lot of unemployed people are in the Clyde district; they are ship-builders. We know that the British government have a fund for sending immigrants to this country and I believe this government anticipates accepting the opportunities afforded by the Imperial authorities in that respect. I have wondered whether it would not be the desire of the Imperial government to get rid of as many of the unemployed over there as possible. But would they be desirable citizens for this country even with the backing of the Canada Colonization Association? Even with the support of this government can we expect those people to come in here and make a success of farming? I do not think it is at all possible, and I believe that even if they did come their experience would be such that in a very short time they would leave this country again.
I might cite as an illustration of what I mean the following: When living at home and thinking that perhaps my neighbour across the road is not enjoying as good a meal as my own menu provides, I might perhaps invite him over and when he comes and sees my fare he turns up his nose. That has been the case with the immigrant coming to this country. He finds out that we have nothing better to offer him than he considers he has at home. The result is that he is discontented and leaves this country as quickly as he possibly can. He finds out that conditions here are not as they were portrayed to him or as he felt he had a right to expect.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would like to ask my hon. friend a question. I am sorry that he has got such an opinion of the proposed assistance that is provided for in the $600,000 that we are going to ask the committee to vote. No portion of that money will be expended except as the result of the nomination by people living in Canada of their friends, .or someone that they know in England, whom they desire to have settle here. We are not indiscriminately offering people the chance to come to Canada. I merely want to put my hon. friend right in that regard.
I thank the minister for his explanation.

speakerposition: topic

speechtext: Are we abrogating the rule in regard to adjourning at 11 o'clock? I notice the hon. member for As-siniboia (Mr. Gould) rose to speak at 11 o'clock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As far as the government is concerned, our desire is to adjourn, if possible, every evening at 11 o'clock, but at present we are not making much progress with the business before the House. I really do not see why these speeches should be made just on the one particular item before us. We should make progress. If the hon. member for Assiniboia has much more to say, we might adjourn at the present time, but we should have it understood that when the committee meets again unless we can make progress with supply, we must continue sitting much later than we have been accustomed to sit. I think everything that it is necessary to say might be said and still permit the business of the House to proceed with a little more expedition.

I do not for one minute object to sitting late. I just want to know where we are. If we are to depart from the 11 o'clock rule I think we should have notice of it. The Prime Minister has told us the next time this order is called we are to expect to sit late, and that progress will have to be made. We are not objecting to that at all. I assume, as no notice has been given of a late sitting to-night, the minister desires to report progress.

I really did not know how long my remarks would take. I have some notes here yet that I might dwell on for some time, but if it is the wish of hon. members that we adjourn, I take pleasure in moving the adjournment of the debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We might adjourn now, and the hon. member could continue his remarks on some other occasion.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King, the House adjourned at 11.35 p.m.
